secs.t: From a third without power to almost none
secs.s: Share of people with access to electricity, India and the peer panel. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s access rose about two points a year for two decades. It passed Pakistan in 2018, drew level with Indonesia by 2021, and stands with Bangladesh at 99.5%. Kenya and Myanmar, at about 76%, are where India was in 2010.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (Tracking SDG 7), 2004–2023.

secs.t: Forty crore people connected
secs.s: Indians without electricity, crore, and India’s share of everyone in the world without it
secs.r: About 40 crore Indians had no electricity in 2004, 20 crore in 2014 and under 1 crore in 2023. In 2004 India was home to 31% of the world’s people without power; by 2023, about 1%. Most of the world’s unconnected now live in sub-Saharan Africa.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI access shares and population.

secs.t: Rural India caught up with the towns
secs.s: Share of people with electricity, rural and urban India
secs.r: Only about half of rural Indians had electricity in 2004. The gap with towns closed by 2023. Two programmes did most of it: village grid extension, which ran under both the UPA and NDA governments, and the Saubhagya household connection drive from 2017, which wired 2.86 crore homes.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; Ministry of Power via SolarQuarter (August 2025).

secs.t: Most villages were reached before 2014; most homes after
secs.s: Villages electrified and homes connected
secs.r: 48,398 villages were electrified from 2009 to 2014 and 18,264 from 2014 to April 2018, when the last inhabited village was declared electrified. Connecting the homes inside those villages came later, through Saubhagya.
secs.src: IndiaSpend (village counts); Ministry of Power via SolarQuarter (Saubhagya).

secs.t: Power now stays on most of the day
secs.s: Average hours of electricity supply per day
secs.r: A connection is only as good as the supply behind it. Rural supply rose from 12.5 hours a day in 2014 to 22.6 in 2025; towns get 23.4. Nationally, the gap between electricity demanded and supplied fell from 4.2% to 0.1%.
secs.src: Ministry of Power reply in Parliament, via The Sentinel (February 2025).

secs.t: Peak demand nearly doubled, and the grid kept up
secs.s: Highest electricity demand met in a single moment, gigawatts; and energy shortage, % of demand
secs.r: Demand peaked at a record 256 GW on 25 April 2026. Transmission lines grew from 2.91 to 4.92 lakh circuit km, and India turned from a net importer of power to a net exporter.
secs.src: Down To Earth (April 2026); Ministry of Power via The Sentinel; Central Electricity Authority (2013–14 peak).

secs.t: India moved past 21 countries
secs.s: Countries with more electricity access than India in 2004 but less in 2023: access in 2004 → 2023
secs.r: India overtook Pakistan, Indonesia, the Philippines, Peru, South Africa and most of Central America. A few, like Libya and Syria, fell back because of war.
secs.src: World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Clean cooking spread fast, but a quarter still burn wood or dung
secs.s: Share of people using clean cooking fuel, mainly LPG, 2004 → 2023
secs.r: India nearly tripled clean cooking, to 77%, a bigger gain than China’s and far ahead of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. In villages it rose from 9% to 66%. The Ujjwala scheme has given 10.35 crore poor households an LPG connection since 2016, but many still cook partly on wood because refills cost money.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO); Ministry of Petroleum via Free Press Journal (December 2025).

secs.t: The grid still loses a seventh of its power
secs.s: Transmission and distribution losses, % of output, 2023
secs.r: Losses fell from 26% in 2004 to 14%, but that is still four times China’s rate and twice Vietnam’s or Bangladesh’s. Theft, unmetered supply and old wires keep state power companies in debt.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (IEA).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: IndiaSpend; World Bank WDI; Ministry of Petroleum via Free Press Journal; Down To Earth.

10.take: India brought electricity to forty crore people and made it reliable in villages. Wires reached almost every home; clean cooking and an efficient grid are still being built.

secs.t: Two rankings, two different countries
secs.s: The ten largest economies in 2024: rank by total GDP and rank by GDP per person, current US dollars. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Every other large economy is also rich or upper-middle income per person. India is the only one of the ten where the average income, $2,695, is below the world median. Brazil, the next poorest of the ten, has almost four times India’s income per person.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, GDP and GDP per capita, current US$, 2024. Per-person rank among 191 countries with 2024 data.

secs.t: The economy climbed seven places; the citizen barely moved
secs.s: India’s rank by size of economy, and the share of countries richer than India per person
secs.r: India rose from 12th to 5th by total output because of its population and steady growth. Per person, about four in five countries were richer than India in 2004 and about three in four still are.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, current US$. The number of countries with data varies from 191 to 212 a year, so the share is used rather than the rank.

secs.t: Behind Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Egypt in income per person
secs.s: GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, current international $, 2004 → 2024
secs.r: Adjusted for prices, the average Indian produces about $11,200 a year, close to the Philippines and Morocco and ahead of Bangladesh, Kenya and Pakistan, but about a third below Vietnam and Indonesia and less than half of China.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, GDP per capita, PPP (current international $).

secs.t: Countries poorer than India live better
secs.s: Human Development Index against income per person, 2023. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan have two-thirds of India’s income per person and higher human development. Morocco and Bangladesh, at a similar income, match or beat it. Vietnam and Sri Lanka, with about 40% more income, score far higher, because their people live longer and stay in school longer.
secs.src: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025, Statistical Annex, Table 1 (GNI per capita in 2021 PPP $).

secs.t: India turns income into wellbeing worse than its income predicts
secs.s: Rank by income per person minus rank by HDI, 2023. Positive: better wellbeing than income would suggest.
secs.r: India ranks seven places lower on human development than on income. Sri Lanka ranks 22 places higher, Kyrgyzstan 24, Vietnam 14 and Nepal 10. These countries get more health and schooling out of each dollar of income.
secs.src: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025, Table 1.

secs.t: Bangladesh started lower and has drawn level
secs.s: Human Development Index, 1990–2023
secs.r: India’s HDI rose by more than half since 1990, from 0.446 to 0.685. Bangladesh rose faster and is now level. China and Vietnam, close to India in 1990, are now far ahead.
secs.src: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025, HDI trends table.

secs.t: The top tenth takes almost three-fifths of national income
secs.s: Shares of national income, 1951 and 2022, and the top 1% share
secs.r: In 1951 the bottom half of Indians earned 20.6% of national income; by 2022, 15%. The top 1% took 22.6% of income and 40.1% of wealth in 2022–23, the highest shares in the record that begins in 1922.
secs.src: World Inequality Lab (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, 2024), via Civilsdaily.

secs.t: Inequality cuts India’s human development by almost a third
secs.s: HDI and HDI adjusted for inequality in health, education and income, 2023
secs.r: Averages hide how unevenly health, schooling and income are shared. Adjusted for that, India’s HDI falls by 30.7%, one of the largest losses in the region.
secs.src: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025, via UNDP India press release (May 2025).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Government of India (December 2025); IMF World Economic Outlook (April 2026) via Basis Point Insight; World Bank WDI; UNDP.

11.take: India grew into one of the world’s largest economies by being large. Per person, it is still a lower-middle-income country that converts income into wellbeing less well than poorer neighbours.

secs.t: Behind every South Asian neighbour except Pakistan and Afghanistan
secs.s: Global Hunger Index 2025 score (lower is better) and rank of 123 countries
secs.r: India’s score of 25.8 puts it in the “serious” band, level with Kenya and Pakistan. Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh are 17 to 41 places ahead. The main drag is child wasting, at 18.7% the second-highest of any country in the report.
secs.src: Global Hunger Index 2025 (Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide). China is ranked jointly in the top group with a score below 5.

secs.t: More food, fewer hungry, but children still short
secs.s: Share of people without enough calories, and foodgrain output
secs.r: Undernourishment, a measure of calories, fell from 22% in 2004 to 12% in 2023. Grain output reached a record 377 million tonnes in 2025–26, and 81 crore people receive free grain each month. Calories are not the same as nutrition: diets heavy in cereals and light in protein, vegetables and fat leave children small even when they are not hungry.
secs.src: FAO via World Bank WDI; Ministry of Agriculture via Agro & Food Processing (2026); PRS India, demand for grants 2026–27.

secs.t: Bangladesh and Nepal started worse and are now better
secs.s: Share of children under five too short for their age (stunted), modelled estimates. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: In 2004 about half of children in India, Bangladesh and Nepal were stunted. By 2024 India had brought it to 33%, Nepal to 26% and Bangladesh to 25%. Progress in India slowed sharply after 2020. Vietnam is at 19%, Sri Lanka at 10% and China at under 5%.
secs.src: UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Joint Malnutrition Estimates, via WDI.

secs.t: Stunting fell; wasting barely moved
secs.s: Children under five, National Family Health Survey rounds
secs.r: Stunting, the long-run marker of poor nutrition, fell from 48% to 35.5% over fifteen years. Underweight fell too. But wasting, the sign of acute hunger or illness, was 19.8% in 2005–06 and 19.3% in 2019–21: one child in five, unchanged.
secs.src: NFHS-3 (2005–06), NFHS-4 (2015–16) and NFHS-5 (2019–21), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

secs.t: The highest child wasting in the peer panel
secs.s: Children under five who are wasted (low weight for height), latest survey year
secs.r: About one Indian child in five is wasted, roughly twice the share in Bangladesh or Sri Lanka and four times Vietnam’s. Only one country among the 123 in the 2025 Global Hunger Index had a higher rate.
secs.src: UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Joint Malnutrition Estimates via WDI; Global Hunger Index 2025.

secs.t: Anaemia is rising, not falling
secs.s: Anaemia among children aged 6–59 months and women aged 15–49, NFHS rounds; and women’s anaemia across the peer panel, 2023
secs.r: Two in three young children and more than half of women were anaemic in 2019–21, up from five years earlier. India’s rate for women, 54% by the WHO’s estimate, is the highest in the peer panel and rising, while Sri Lanka, Indonesia and China have brought theirs down.
secs.src: NFHS-3, 4 and 5, via Down To Earth; WHO via World Bank WDI (women 15–49, 2023).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Ministry of Women and Child Development (Poshan Tracker) via The Week (July 2025); NFHS-5; Global Hunger Index 2025.

12.take: India has largely solved hunger for calories. It has not solved nutrition: wasting has not moved in fifteen years, anaemia is rising, and smaller neighbours now feed their children better.

leap.n: of 123 countries, behind Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka

secs.t: Less spent on health than most peers, and shorter lives than several
secs.s: Health spending as a share of GDP (2023) against life expectancy (2024). Circle size: spending per person. Tap or hover a circle.
secs.r: India spends 3.3% of its economy on health, less than Nepal, Vietnam, Kenya, the Philippines or Morocco. Sri Lanka spends about the same share and its people live more than five years longer. Bangladesh spends even less, relies heavily on community health workers, and outlives India by 2.7 years.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO Global Health Expenditure Database; UN population estimates).

secs.t: India’s health share fell as China’s, Nepal’s and Morocco’s rose
secs.s: Current health expenditure, % of GDP, 2004–2023. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Total health spending fell from 4.0% of GDP in 2004 to under 3% before the pandemic and 3.3% in 2023. India’s world rank on this measure fell from 145th to 170th of about 190 countries. China went from about the same share as India to almost 6%.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO).

secs.t: The government still spends just 1.3% of GDP on health
secs.s: Government health spending, % of GDP, 2004 → 2023
secs.r: Public spending nearly doubled as a share of GDP but remains half the 2.5% target set by the National Health Policy of 2017 for 2025. China’s government spends 3.4%, Morocco’s 3.4% and Vietnam’s 2%. India ranks 153rd of 192 countries.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO). India’s own National Health Accounts put it higher; see the contested numbers below.

secs.t: Out-of-pocket payments fell, but still cover over two-fifths of the bill
secs.s: Share of health spending paid directly by patients, 2004 → 2023
secs.r: In 2004 Indians paid 72% of their health costs themselves; by 2023, 44%. That is real progress, helped by insurance schemes and free medicines. But it remains above China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Kenya, where patients pay a quarter to two-fifths. Bangladesh, at 79%, has moved the other way.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO).

secs.t: About $350 a year per person on health
secs.s: Health spending per person, international $ at purchasing-power parity, 2023
secs.r: Adjusted for prices, India spends about half what Vietnam spends per person and less than a quarter of China. It spends more than poorer Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Kenya and Myanmar, and less than Indonesia, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Morocco.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO).

secs.t: Bangladeshis now live 2.7 years longer than Indians
secs.s: Life expectancy at birth, years, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India and Bangladesh had the same life expectancy in 2004, about 64.5 years. Bangladesh pulled ahead and the pandemic widened the gap: India lost about three years of life expectancy in 2021. Sri Lanka and China are more than five years ahead.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (UN World Population Prospects).

secs.t: Fewer hospital beds per person than in 2004; wider coverage of basic services
secs.s: Hospital beds per 1,000 people, and the WHO index of essential health service coverage (0–100)
secs.r: Hospital beds did not keep up with population: 2.0 per 1,000 people in 2004, 1.6 in 2021, against 5.6 in China and 3.9 in Sri Lanka. Coverage of essential services, such as vaccination, antenatal care and TB treatment, rose from 41 to 69 out of 100, lifting India from 140th to 116th of 193 countries.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO).

secs.t: One of the world’s largest public health insurance schemes
secs.r: Ayushman Bharat pays for hospital care for poorer families. In eight years it funded 13.25 crore admissions worth ₹2.03 lakh crore. It covers hospital stays, not the doctor visits and medicines that make up most out-of-pocket spending.
secs.src: National Health Authority via Digital Health News (September 2026).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: National Health Accounts 2021–22 via IAS Gyan; WHO via WDI; Ministry of Health in Parliament and FactChecker (2022).

13.take: India kept health on a shoestring while its economy boomed. People live longer, mostly because of cheaper wins like vaccines and safer births; the system to treat adults has not been built at the same pace.

leap.n: of GDP, 2004 to 2023; target was 2.5% by 2025

secs.t: Fewer than one in four can read a Class 2 story
secs.s: Class 3 children in rural government schools who can read a Class 2 text. One figure = one child in a class of 100.
secs.r: The share fell during the school closures of 2020–22 and recovered to 23.4% in 2024, above its level before the pandemic. Even so, three in four children reach Class 3 unable to read a text meant for Class 2.
secs.src: ASER Centre, Annual Status of Education Report (Rural) 2018, 2022, 2024, via Careers360.

secs.t: By Class 8, a third still cannot read a Class 2 text
secs.s: Rural children who can do Class 2-level reading or basic arithmetic, by class, 2024
secs.r: Children improve as they move up, but slowly. Fewer than half of Class 5 children in government schools read at Class 2 level, and fewer than one in three can do a simple division. In Class 8, 54% cannot do basic arithmetic.
secs.src: ASER 2024 via Careers360. Reading for Classes 3, 5 and 8 and Class 3 subtraction refer to government schools; Class 5 division and Class 8 arithmetic to all rural schools.

secs.t: Enrolment rose fast, but some poorer neighbours enrol more
secs.s: Gross secondary enrolment ratio, %, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s secondary enrolment rose from 53% to 78%. Nepal, Kenya and Morocco, all poorer or similar per person, now enrol 84–90%. Youth literacy reached 97%, but literacy measures whether someone can read a sentence, not whether they learned in school.
secs.src: UNESCO Institute for Statistics, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: More than half of 10-year-olds cannot read and understand a simple text
secs.s: World Bank “learning poverty”: share of children who cannot read and understand an age-appropriate text by age 10, latest year
secs.r: India’s learning poverty, 56%, is three times Vietnam’s or China’s and almost four times Sri Lanka’s. It is level with Bangladesh and Indonesia and better than Pakistan, Kenya and the Philippines.
secs.src: World Bank and UNESCO Institute for Statistics, via WDI. Latest year per country.

secs.t: The national survey finds the same gaps
secs.s: PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, 21 lakh students in 74,000 schools
secs.r: The Ministry of Education’s own survey found Class 6 students answered 46% of mathematics questions correctly, and only 53% knew their tables up to 10. In Class 3, 58% could add and subtract two-digit numbers.
secs.src: Ministry of Education, PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, via The Week (PTI, July 2025).

secs.t: India spends more on schooling than most peers
secs.s: Public spending on education, % of GDP, latest year
secs.r: India spends about 4% of GDP on education, more than Vietnam, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or China’s reported share, though below the 6% target in the National Education Policy. Money is not the main gap: Vietnam spends less and its children learn far more.
secs.src: UNESCO Institute for Statistics, via WDI. Latest year per country.

secs.t: One in three young people in higher education
secs.s: Gross tertiary enrolment ratio, %, latest year
secs.r: Higher-education enrolment tripled from 11% in 2004 to 34%. China went from 17% to 77% over the same years; Morocco, the Philippines and Indonesia are all above 44%.
secs.src: UNESCO Institute for Statistics, via WDI.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: World Bank WDI; ASER 2024; The Better India (PISA 2009); National Education Policy 2020.

14.take: India solved getting children into school. It has not solved getting them to learn: most leave primary school unable to read well or do simple arithmetic, a gap spending alone has not closed.

leap.k: Class 3, govt schools, can read a Class 2 text

leap.n: of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, 2017

secs.t: At India’s income, most countries had more factories and more women at work
secs.s: 53 countries at the moment their income per person matched India’s 2024 level: manufacturing share of GDP against women’s labour-force participation. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: At India’s level of income, the typical country had 15% of its economy in manufacturing and 48% of women in the labour force. India has 12.6% and 32%. China, when it was as rich as India is now, had 31% in manufacturing and 64% of women working. Factories are the usual route by which women and farm workers enter paid work.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; income per person at PPP (constant 2021 international $). For each country, the year between 1990 and 2024 when its income was closest to India’s 2024 level, within 12%.

secs.t: Bangladesh and Vietnam built factories; India’s share fell
secs.s: Manufacturing value added, % of GDP, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s share peaked at 17% in 2010 and has fallen since. Bangladesh rose from 14% to 22% on garments, Vietnam from 17% to 24% on electronics. China and Indonesia fell too, but from far higher levels.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (national accounts). Vietnam and China series start later or are rebased.

secs.t: Nineteen countries moved past India
secs.s: Countries with a smaller manufacturing share than India in 2004 but a larger one in 2024: share in 2004 → 2024
secs.r: Some passed India by building industry, like Bangladesh, Uganda and Pakistan; others because India’s own share fell, like Russia and Tunisia, whose shares also declined.
secs.src: World Bank WDI.

secs.t: India makes under 4% of the world’s manufactured goods
secs.s: Share of world manufacturing value added, current US$
secs.r: India’s share of world manufacturing more than doubled, from 1.6% to 3.6%, because its economy grew. China’s went from 9% to 36% over the same years.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI, manufacturing value added (current US$), countries with data.

secs.t: Vietnam, with a fourteenth of India’s people, exports almost as many goods
secs.s: Goods exports, US$ billion, and share of world goods exports
secs.r: India’s goods exports grew from $78 billion in 2004 to $447 billion in 2024, but its share of world trade has been stuck below 2% for a decade. Vietnam’s grew from $26 billion to $407 billion.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (balance of payments, goods exports, current US$).

secs.t: Four in ten Indians still work on farms
secs.s: Share of workers in agriculture, 2004 → 2024 (ILO modelled estimates)
secs.r: The farm share of work fell from 56% to 42%, but it rose again after 2019 as workers returned to villages. Industry’s share rose from 18% to 25%, much of it in construction rather than factories. In Vietnam, China and Indonesia fewer than three in ten now work on farms.
secs.src: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via WDI.

secs.t: Smartphones became one of India’s largest exports
secs.r: Production-linked incentives drew Apple’s suppliers to India. iPhones are now India’s largest branded export. Much of the value of each phone is still in imported components; assembly creates jobs but less domestic value than the headline numbers suggest.
secs.src: Business Today (April 2026); Reuters via Malay Mail (March 2025).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Make in India (2014); Reuters via Malay Mail (March 2025); World Bank WDI; Ashoka University ICPP (2026).

15.take: India skipped the factory stage that lifted China, Vietnam and Bangladesh. Without it, farm workers and women have had few good jobs to move into.

secs.t: Almost every woman got a bank account; most still have no job
secs.s: Indian women aged 15+: share with an account at a bank or mobile-money provider, and share in the labour force. Tap or hover a point.
secs.r: Jan Dhan accounts and direct benefit transfers took women’s account ownership from about a quarter to nine in ten, level with China. Over the same years the share of women working or looking for work fell from 35% to a low of 26% in 2020, and has only partly recovered. An account is useful when there is income to put in it.
secs.src: World Bank Global Findex, via WDI (accounts); International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via WDI (labour force).

secs.t: Bangladesh’s women went to work; India’s went home, then partly came back
secs.s: Women’s labour-force participation, % of women aged 15+, 2004–2025. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: In 2004 India was ahead of Bangladesh. Garment factories then drew millions of Bangladeshi women into paid work, and Bangladesh moved ahead by 2008. India’s rate slid for fifteen years, through a period of fast growth, before rising after 2020. Vietnam and China, where factory jobs came early, are near 60–70%.
secs.src: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Only twenty countries have a smaller share of women in the labour force
secs.s: Women’s labour-force participation, 2024, 180 countries. Each dot is a country; colour shows region. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: The typical country has 54% of its women in the labour force. Most of the countries below India are in the Middle East and North Africa, or are at war: Yemen, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Iran, Egypt. Pakistan and Nepal are lower; Sri Lanka has slipped just below India since its 2022 crisis.
secs.src: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI. Countries with data for 2024.

secs.k: The gap between men and women
secs.t: Men work at about the same rate everywhere; women make the difference
secs.s: Labour-force participation, 2024: women and men aged 15+. Sorted by the gap. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: Indian men are in the labour force at much the same rate as men in Vietnam, Indonesia or Bangladesh. The difference between these countries is almost entirely about women. India’s gap of 45 percentage points is among the widest; only Pakistan’s is wider in this group.
secs.src: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: One in five working Indian women earns a wage; one in three is an unpaid family helper
secs.s: Employed women by type of work, 2024, %
secs.r: Of the women who do work, most in India work on their family’s farm or in a household business, often unpaid. In Bangladesh unpaid family work fell from 68% of working women to 12% in twenty years as factory jobs grew. In India the share barely moved.
secs.src: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Much of the recent rise is unpaid work on family farms
secs.s: India’s official survey shows a much sharper rise than the international estimate
secs.r: India’s Periodic Labour Force Survey shows women’s participation nearly doubling, to 41.7% in 2023–24. Most of the rise was in villages, and much of it was women counted as helpers in family enterprises, mostly farms. The share of working women in regular salaried jobs fell over the same years, from 21% to 16%.
secs.src: MoSPI, PLFS Annual Report 2023–24; Foundation for Agrarian Studies analysis of PLFS unit data (helpers); Business Standard analysis of PLFS (salaried share).

secs.t: Four times as many women go to college; four in ten young women are not in work or study
secs.s: Women’s college enrolment in India, and young women (15–24) not in employment, education or training
secs.r: Women’s enrolment in higher education rose from 9% to 35% of their age group, slightly above the rate for men. Yet 39% of young Indian women are neither working nor studying, against 20% in Bangladesh and 11% in Vietnam. Education has not turned into jobs.
secs.src: UNESCO and ILO, via World Bank WDI. Latest year shown in brackets.

secs.t: Women do more than three times the unpaid housework men do
secs.s: India’s Time Use Survey, 2024
secs.r: The average Indian woman spends nearly five hours a day on cooking, cleaning and other unpaid housework; the average man spends an hour and a half. On a given day only a quarter of women aged 15–59 did any paid work, against three-quarters of men. Childcare, safe transport and work close to home decide whether women can take a job.
secs.src: MoSPI, Time Use Survey 2024, via Business Today. Minutes are averages per person aged 6 and above; participation is for ages 15–59.

secs.t: Fewer girls are being lost before birth, but the gap has not closed
secs.s: Boys born per 100 girls, 2004–2024. Without sex selection the ratio is about 105. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s sex ratio at birth has improved from 109 boys per 100 girls to 107, as the ban on sex-selective scans was enforced more strictly and the Beti Bachao campaign began in 2015. China has improved faster from a worse start; Vietnam has got worse. The UN estimated in 2020 that 45.8 million females were “missing” from India’s population, through sex selection before birth and neglect after it.
secs.src: UN World Population Prospects, via World Bank WDI; UNFPA, State of World Population 2020.

secs.t: Fewer than one MP in seven is a woman
secs.s: Women’s share of seats in the lower or single house of parliament, latest year
secs.r: Women hold 13.8% of seats in the Lok Sabha, up from 8.3% in 2004 but behind Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan, which reserve seats for women, and Vietnam, which sets a quota for women candidates. India passed a law in 2023 to reserve a third of seats, but it takes effect only after the next census and a redrawing of constituencies.
secs.src: Inter-Parliamentary Union, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: MoSPI PLFS 2023–24; ILO via WDI; Ministry of Finance (Jan Dhan, August 2025); World Bank Global Findex 2025, via Moneylife; Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023.

16.take: India gave women accounts, phones and transfers, but not jobs. Bringing women into paid work is the largest untapped source of growth India has.

leap.k: Countries with fewer women at work

secs.t: Road deaths almost doubled in twenty years
secs.s: People killed in road crashes in India, as reported by police, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Deaths rose every year until 2011, held near 1.4–1.5 lakh for most of the 2010s, dipped during the 2020 lockdown, and have set a new record each year since. The 2019 law that raised traffic fines up to tenfold did not reverse the trend.
secs.src: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), Road Accidents in India, annual reports; 2024 from MoRTH via ETV Bharat.

secs.t: The world began cutting road deaths; India did not
secs.s: Road deaths indexed to 2010 = 100. India: reported deaths, every year. World: WHO estimates for 2010 and 2021.
secs.r: Between 2010 and 2021 road deaths worldwide fell 5%, to 1.19 million a year, even as the number of vehicles grew. Ten countries, including Japan, Norway and the UAE, more than halved theirs. India’s reported deaths rose 14% over the same years, and kept rising to 2024.
secs.src: WHO, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023, via Deccan Herald; MoRTH.

secs.t: India’s death rate is middling, but it has not fallen
secs.s: WHO-modelled road deaths per 100,000 people, 2004 → 2019. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: Measured per person, India is not an outlier: by WHO’s model its rate of 15.6 is below the world’s and below the typical country at its income. What stands out is that it did not move in fifteen years. China, Brazil, Morocco and Thailand cut their rates by between a sixth and nearly a third; Japan and Britain by more than half.
secs.src: WHO Global Health Estimates, via World Bank WDI. WHO’s modelled estimates are higher than India’s police-reported count.

secs.t: 115 of 183 countries made their roads safer; India stayed where it was
secs.s: Change in road deaths per 100,000 people, 2004 to 2019. Each dot is a country. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: Most countries, rich and poor, lowered their road death rate as they grew. India’s change was zero to one decimal place. Its large and growing population means that a flat rate still produces more deaths each year.
secs.src: WHO Global Health Estimates, via World Bank WDI. “Little change” is within 0.5 deaths per 100,000.

secs.t: Two in three of the dead were on two wheels or on foot
secs.s: Road deaths in 2024 by road user: 100 squares, one for each 1%
secs.r: Indian roads are built for cars and trucks but used mostly by people on scooters, motorcycles and foot. Two-wheeler riders were 46% of the dead and pedestrians 21%. Two-thirds of those killed in 2023 were aged 18 to 45, in their working years.
secs.src: MoRTH, Road Accidents in India 2024, via ETV Bharat; age share from the 2023 report, via NEXT IAS.

secs.t: Speed, and no helmet
secs.s: Causes recorded in police reports, 2023
secs.r: Police attribute two-thirds of deaths to overspeeding. More than 54,000 people died without a helmet and 16,000 without a seatbelt, though both are compulsory. Nearly one death in five was a hit-and-run. These are failures of enforcement, not of law.
secs.src: MoRTH, Road Accidents in India 2023, via The Week / PTI.

secs.t: National highways are 2% of roads and carry over a third of the deaths
secs.s: National highways’ share of road length, traffic and deaths; and road deaths by type of road, 2024
secs.r: National highways carry about 40% of all road traffic, so their share of deaths roughly matches their share of traffic. The problem is how they are used: fast trucks and cars share lanes with two-wheelers, tractors and people on foot, often with no crossing for kilometres.
secs.src: MoRTH via ETV Bharat (deaths by road type); MoRTH via Anantam IAS (road length and traffic share).

secs.t: India’s official count may miss a third to a half of road deaths
secs.s: Police-reported deaths against WHO estimates for the same year
secs.r: Police records miss deaths that occur later in hospital, or that are never reported. WHO’s 2018 report put India’s road deaths at about 3 lakh in 2016, twice the official count. WHO’s newer model is lower but still about 43% above the police figure for 2019. Whatever the true number, it is higher than the one that guides policy.
secs.src: WHO, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2018, India country profile; WHO Global Health Estimates via WDI, multiplied by population; MoRTH.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Business Today (February 2021); Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019; UN General Assembly resolution 74/299 (2020); MoRTH.

17.take: India built roads at record speed but did not make them safe. The roads became faster; enforcement, crossings and trauma care did not keep up.

secs.t: Only five countries recorded dirtier air than India in 2025
secs.s: Annual average PM2.5, µg/m³, population-weighted, from ground monitors, 2025
secs.r: India’s average fell 3% in 2025, to 48.9 µg/m³. That is still nearly ten times the WHO guideline and above India’s own, much looser, standard of 40. Its neighbours Pakistan and Bangladesh are worse: the air of the Indo-Gangetic plain does not stop at borders.
secs.src: IQAir, World Air Quality Report 2025, via IQAir and Vajiram & Ravi. WHO guideline: 5 µg/m³; India’s national standard: 40 µg/m³.

secs.t: Almost every poor country breathes cleaner air than India
secs.s: Annual exposure to PM2.5, 2019, WHO-modelled estimates for 198 countries. Each dot is a country; colour shows income group. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: On WHO’s model, India had the seventh-dirtiest air of 198 countries in 2019. Most of those ahead of it are desert states whose air is thick with natural dust, such as Qatar, Niger and Mauritania. Thirty of 31 low-income countries had cleaner air than India; the typical one was at 36 µg/m³ against India’s 60.
secs.src: WHO/Global Burden of Disease estimates, via World Bank WDI. Satellite-based model; values differ from monitor averages.

secs.t: Kenya, Ethiopia and Rwanda breathe far cleaner air
secs.s: Annual exposure to PM2.5, 2019, µg/m³ (WHO-modelled)
secs.r: Countries far poorer than India, and still burning wood and charcoal, have cleaner outdoor air. India’s problem is the scale of what is burned on a crowded plain: coal in power plants and factories, diesel, crop stubble, household fuel and construction dust, trapped by winter weather in the north.
secs.src: WHO/Global Burden of Disease estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Two of every three of the world’s most polluted cities are Indian
secs.s: The 100 most polluted cities in the world, 2025: one square per city
secs.r: The most polluted city in the world in 2025 was Loni, on the edge of Delhi, at 112.5 µg/m³. Byrnihat in Meghalaya and New Delhi followed among Indian cities. Delhi, at 82.2, was at a three-year low and was still the most polluted capital in the world.
secs.src: IQAir, World Air Quality Report 2025.

secs.t: Dirty air is the biggest single threat to life in South Asia
secs.r: Air pollution was linked to about 2.1 million deaths in India in 2021, including some 1.7 lakh children under five. It is the leading risk factor for death in South Asia, ahead of high blood pressure, poor diet and tobacco.
secs.src: Health Effects Institute, State of Global Air 2024, via The South First.

secs.t: The average Indian loses three and a half years of life to dirty air; a Delhi resident eight
secs.s: Life expectancy lost compared with air that meets the WHO guideline, years, 2023
secs.r: The University of Chicago’s Air Quality Life Index estimates how much longer people would live if the air met WHO’s guideline. Indians would gain 3.5 years on average, almost double the global figure. In Delhi the gain would be 8.2 years; meeting just India’s own standard would add 4.7.
secs.src: Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago, Air Quality Life Index 2025.

secs.t: Clean cooking fuel reached most homes, and cut smoke indoors
secs.s: Share of people mainly cooking with clean fuels such as LPG, gas or electricity, %, 2004–2023. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Ujjwala connections, launched in 2016, took LPG to poor rural households. Three Indians in four now cook mainly with clean fuel, up from about one in four in 2004; in villages the share rose from 9% to 66%. India moved well ahead of Pakistan and Bangladesh. Many households still also burn wood when cylinders run out, and outdoor air has not improved to match.
secs.src: WHO, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Most cities missed their clean-air targets; most money went on road dust
secs.s: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), launched 2019: results to 2025–26 in cities with adequate data, and how the money was spent
secs.r: NCAP asked 130 cities to cut coarse dust (PM10) by 20–30% from 2017–18 levels, later raised to 40%. Of 100 cities with enough data, 23 met the 40% target and 23 got worse. Two-thirds of the money went to sweeping and sprinkling roads, while industry, vehicles and crop burning, among the main sources of the finest and deadliest particles, received far less.
secs.src: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), Tracing the Hazy Air 2026.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: IQAir 2025; CREA 2026; WHO Air Quality Guidelines (2021); Central Pollution Control Board standards (2009).

18.take: India cleaned its power supply faster than its air. Clean air needs action on coal, diesel, stubble and dust across whole regions, not city by city.

leap.n: µg/m³, nearly 10 times the WHO guideline of 5

secs.t: Of every 100 litres of urban sewage, 28 are treated
secs.s: India’s urban sewage, million litres a day (MLD): generated, treatment capacity built, capacity working, and sewage actually treated. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Indian cities produce about 72,000 million litres of sewage a day. Plants exist to treat 44% of it; some of those plants are not working, and the rest run below capacity, so about 28% is treated. The other 52,000 million litres a day flow into drains, rivers, lakes and the ground.
secs.src: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), national inventory of sewage treatment plants, 2021, via Down To Earth. The latest national count.

secs.t: The Yamuna enters Delhi within the safe limit and leaves it 3,160 times over
secs.s: Faecal coliform bacteria in the Yamuna, November 2024, MPN per 100 ml. Logarithmic scale: each step is ten times the last.
secs.r: At Palla, where it enters Delhi, the river carried 1,100 faecal bacteria per 100 ml, under the bathing limit of 2,500. By Asgarpur, about 50 km downstream, after more than 20 large drains have emptied into it, the count was 79 lakh. Six of eight sampling points had no dissolved oxygen at all in May 2025.
secs.src: Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) monitoring, via The Week / PTI (December 2024) and ETV Bharat (May 2025). Limit: CPCB maximum permissible for bathing, 2,500 MPN/100 ml.

secs.t: Delhi has the plants but not the results
secs.s: Delhi’s sewage, million litres a day, 2025: what meets the discharge standard, what is treated badly, and what is not treated
secs.r: Delhi’s 37 plants could in theory treat almost all of the 3,596 million litres a day the city produces. In practice, 14 of the plants fail the discharge standard and 641 million litres a day bypass treatment altogether. Nine completed Namami Gange projects in Delhi cost ₹1,951 crore.
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti reply in Lok Sabha, July 2025, via The Week / PTI. “Fails the standard” is the remainder after the treated-to-standard and untreated volumes.

secs.t: Fewer polluted stretches, but nearly 300 remain
secs.s: River stretches classed as polluted by CPCB (BOD above 3 mg/l), by assessment year
secs.r: The count of polluted river stretches fell from 351 in 2018 to 296 in 2025, on 271 rivers. Twenty-five are in the worst class, with oxygen demand more than ten times the bathing limit, and 85 were unchanged.
secs.src: CPCB, Polluted River Stretches for Restoration of Water Quality (2018, 2022, 2025), via The Policy Edge.

secs.t: On safely managed sanitation, India is above the average for its income
secs.s: Share of people using a toilet whose waste is safely disposed of or treated, %, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: The international measure counts a household as safely served when its waste is treated, either at a plant or in a well-built septic tank or pit. On that measure India rose from 17% to 63%, ahead of the 49% typical for lower-middle-income countries and of Bangladesh and Kenya. Most Indian toilets drain to tanks and pits, which is why the rivers can stay foul while the sanitation figure improves.
secs.src: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Dirty water still kills Indians at twice the rate of their neighbours
secs.s: Deaths from unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene, per lakh people, 2019 (WHO)
secs.r: India ranked 30th worst of 183 countries. Every country with a higher rate is in Africa, except Pakistan and Kiribati. India’s rate is twice Bangladesh’s and Nepal’s, and about 16 times China’s. Toilets reduce exposure only if the waste does not come back through drinking water, food and floods.
secs.src: WHO, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Nearly 500 workers have died in sewers and septic tanks since 2019
secs.s: Deaths while cleaning sewers and septic tanks, by year (2026: January to June)
secs.r: Workers, mostly from Dalit communities, are still sent into tanks and drains without protective gear, despite a 2013 law banning manual scavenging and court orders for mechanised cleaning. The government counts these as sewer deaths, not manual scavenging, and reports no deaths from manual scavenging.
secs.src: Ministry of Social Justice reply in Lok Sabha, August 2026, citing the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis, via Business Standard.

secs.t: Taps reached four rural homes in five; the waste water from them has nowhere to go
secs.r: Jal Jeevan Mission raised rural tap connections from 3.2 crore homes in 2019 to more than 15.4 crore by early 2025. More piped water means more waste water. Without drains and treatment in villages and small towns, it collects in streets and ponds or seeps into the groundwater that many still drink.
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti via All India Radio News (February 2025); CPCB 2021.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: CPCB (2021); Lok Sabha replies (July 2025, August 2026); CPCB Polluted River Stretches (2025).

19.take: India built toilets but not the system behind them. Sewers, working treatment plants and faecal-sludge services are the unglamorous second half of the sanitation mission.

leap.n: the safe limit for faecal bacteria, Nov 2024

leap.k: Deaths from unsafe water and sanitation

secs.t: Nine claims, nine checks
secs.s: Each row compares an official figure with an independent or more complete measure of the same thing. Bars are scaled within each row. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Some gaps come from definitions: a village counted as electrified when a tenth of its homes had power, sewage counted as handled when a plant was built. Others come from what is counted: police records of road deaths, anganwadi registers for child wasting. In every case the official figure is the more flattering one.
secs.src: see the earlier chapters on each topic; MoHUA and CPCB via Scroll (waste); Arvind Subramanian, Harvard CID (2019), via The Wire (GDP).

secs.t: Nepal and India were both declared free of open defecation in 2019. Only Nepal got there.
secs.s: People practising open defecation, % of population, 2004–2024 (WHO/UNICEF). Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s fall from 62% to under 7% is a real achievement. But the 2019 declaration came when about a fifth of Indians were still going in the open, and five years later one in fifteen still were, about ten crore people. Bangladesh, Vietnam and Sri Lanka reached zero quietly; Nepal reached almost zero after its own declaration.
secs.src: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Three-quarters processed, according to the ministry; less than half, according to the pollution board
secs.s: Urban solid waste: the ministry’s claim, and CPCB’s breakdown for 2020–21, % of waste generated
secs.r: In 2022 a minister told Parliament that 73% of India’s solid waste was processed; by 2024 the ministry said 80%. The Central Pollution Control Board’s own report for 2020–21 found 47% treated, 27% dumped in landfills and a quarter not accounted for at all. The two count differently: the ministry adds up processing capacity and city claims; the board compiles what state pollution boards report as actually treated.
secs.src: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and CPCB Annual Report 2020–21, via Scroll (August 2022); MoHUA data in Parliament, via iamrenew (2024).

secs.t: The surveys that could check the claims ran late, or did not appear
secs.s: When key national statistics were collected, 2004–2027. Red bars show gaps; a cross marks data collected but withheld.
secs.r: The Census due in 2021 was postponed and will count people on 1 March 2027, sixteen years after the last one. The 2017–18 consumption survey, which a leaked draft suggested showed falling rural spending, was withheld for “data quality” reasons. No official poverty count has been published since 2011–12. India left the OECD’s PISA learning test after 2009. Policy for a sixth of humanity has been run on old denominators.
secs.src: Registrar General of India notification, via The South First; MoSPI; NFHS reports; OECD PISA. The 2017–18 consumption survey was withheld in November 2019.

secs.t: When outside measures disagreed, the response was often to reject the measure
secs.r: The government has called the Global Hunger Index flawed, attributed the 2009 PISA result to “out of context” questions, and had its economic advisers dismiss research suggesting growth was overstated. Some criticisms have merit, but the rejected numbers were rarely replaced with better ones.
secs.src: Global Hunger Index 2025; OECD PISA 2009+; EAC-PM response to Subramanian (2019), via The Week; Harvard CID.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Arvind Subramanian (2019), via The Wire; Registrar General of India; The Quint (November 2019) on the withheld consumption survey.

20.take: A target declared met is not the same as a target met. The fix is not better announcements but numbers citizens can check: independent statistics, published on time, including the ones that disappoint.

leap.n: 6.7% still in the open in 2024, ≈10 crore people

secs.t: Income concentration fell for thirty years after independence, then rose past colonial levels
secs.s: Share of national income going to the top 10%, India, selected years
secs.r: The top tenth’s share fell from 37% in 1951 to 30% by 1982, under planning, high taxes and land reform. It has risen since liberalisation, and fastest after 2014, to about 58% in 2022–23. On this measure India’s top 1% now takes a larger share than in the United States, Brazil or South Africa.
secs.src: Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, “Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922–2023: The Rise of the Billionaire Raj”, World Inequality Lab (2024), as reported by Madhyamam. Only the three published points are plotted; the line joins them.

secs.t: The top 1% earn 23 times the average Indian; the bottom half share 15%
secs.s: Share of national income and of wealth, 2022–23
secs.r: The poorer half of Indian adults, some 46 crore people, receive about 15% of national income. The top 1%, about 90 lakh adults, receive 22.6% and own 40% of the wealth. Their average income, about ₹53 lakh a year, is 23 times the national average.
secs.src: World Inequality Lab (2024), as above.

secs.t: Household surveys show India as one of the more equal countries; income and tax records show the opposite
secs.s: Share of the top 10%, latest year: household surveys for all countries (World Bank), and India’s share of national income from tax and national accounts (World Inequality Lab)
secs.r: The government’s consumption survey puts India’s Gini coefficient at 25.5 in 2022–23, among the lowest in the world, with the top tenth accounting for 22% of spending. Surveys measure spending, not income, and miss most of the very rich, who neither answer surveys nor spend most of what they earn. Tax and national-accounts data capture them, and show a top tenth with 58% of income. Both can be true; only one describes who is pulling ahead.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (survey-based Gini and top-decile share, 2022); World Inequality Lab (2024).

secs.t: 284 billionaires hold wealth worth almost a third of India’s annual output
secs.r: Hurun counted 284 Indian billionaires in 2025, with combined wealth of ₹98 lakh crore, about 30% of a year’s GDP. A 2% annual tax on the net wealth of the 167 richest families alone would, the World Inequality Lab estimates, raise about 0.5% of national income, more than a third of what India’s governments spend on public health in a year.
secs.src: Hurun Global Rich List 2025, via IANS; World Inequality Lab (2024); GDP from World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Recorded riots fell; protests by prosperous groups for quotas grew
secs.s: Rioting cases registered by police, 2014–2020, and quota agitations by landowning groups
secs.r: Inequality has not, on police records, brought more rioting: registered riot cases fell by about 30% between 2014 and 2019, though they rose again in 2020 with the Delhi violence. The strain shows elsewhere. Jats in Haryana, Patidars in Gujarat and Marathas in Maharashtra, traditionally landowning and politically powerful, have mounted mass agitations to be classed as backward for quotas in government jobs and colleges. Their grievance is not destitution but falling behind: farm incomes stagnant, and too few good jobs for their children.
secs.src: NCRB, Crime in India, via Factly; Shankar IAS Parliament on “competitive backwardness” (2017); ORF.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: World Bank WDI; World Inequality Lab (2024); NCRB via Factly.

21.take: Growth that pools at the top weakens the bargain that holds a diverse democracy together: that effort pays and the system is fair. India’s strains show as quota fights and resentment more than riots, but they are a warning, not a fixed state.

leap.n: for the poorer half of adults

secs.t: An average person in Delhi earns eight times as much as one in Bihar
secs.s: Net state domestic product per person, ₹ thousand, current prices, 2023–24 (2022–23 where marked). Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: The southern and western states and Delhi earn three to eight times as much per person as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. These three poorest states hold over a quarter of India’s people and send the most migrants to the richer ones.
secs.src: Economic Survey 2023–24, Statistical Appendix Table 1.11A (state statistical offices).

secs.t: The big southern states are pulling further ahead of Bihar
secs.s: Income per head as a multiple of Bihar’s, 2015–16 and 2022–23, current prices
secs.r: Telangana went from 4.6 to 5.8 times Bihar’s income per head in seven years, and Karnataka from 4.9 to 5.6. Uttar Pradesh stood still relative to Bihar. Small, rich Goa and Delhi converged a little, but the large states that hold most people are diverging.
secs.src: Economic Survey 2023–24, Table 1.11A; multiples computed from rupee values.

secs.t: Half of tribal Indians and a third of Dalits and Muslims are multidimensionally poor
secs.s: Share of each group deprived in health, schooling and living standards, %, 2015–16 (NFHS-4)
secs.r: Deprivation tracks caste and faith closely. Tribal poverty fell fast, from about 80% in 2005–06, yet in 2015–16 a tribal Indian was still more than three times as likely to be poor as an upper-caste one. Five in six of India’s multidimensionally poor came from Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes or Other Backward Classes.
secs.src: UNDP–OPHI Global MPI 2018 and 2021, via ThePrint and ForumIAS.

secs.t: Upper-caste Hindus own 41% of household wealth with 22% of the people
secs.s: Share of national household wealth vs share of population, %, by group
secs.r: Wealth is more unequal than income because it is inherited: land, houses and businesses pass down family lines. Scheduled Castes and Tribes, over a quarter of the people, hold about a ninth of the wealth; Muslims, about an eighth of households, hold 8%.
secs.src: SPPU, JNU and Indian Institute of Dalit Studies, “Wealth Ownership and Inequality in India” (NSSO data), via Business Today.

secs.t: Gaps that follow identity reward identity politics and cash handouts
secs.s: Three signals of how parties respond to uneven growth
secs.r: When a group is visibly behind, a party can win its vote by promising quotas, grievance or a monthly cash transfer, all faster than building schools and jobs. The number of states paying women unconditionally rose from 2 to 12 in three years; hate-speech events recorded by one monitoring group rose 74% in 2024, a third of them during the election campaign; and the share of Muslim MPs is at a historic low. Each response is rational for a party and costly for the country.
secs.src: Factly (Lok Sabha); India Hate Lab, Hate Speech Events in India 2024; PRS Legislative Research via Deccan Herald.

secs.t: Manipur: a fight over quotas and land turned into three years of killing
secs.s: Ethnic violence between Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities, since 3 May 2023
secs.r: The violence began after a court order on granting the Meitei majority tribal status, which Kuki-Zo groups saw as a threat to their land and job reservations. A dispute over shares of a slow-growing state economy became a conflict that emptied whole districts of one community or the other.
secs.src: Manipur Home Minister to the Assembly, via The Pioneer (deaths, missing); state home department, via Amar Ujala (displaced).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: UNDP–OPHI Global MPI; PRS; India Hate Lab.

22.take: Uneven growth would be a problem anywhere. In India it falls along lines of caste, faith and region, which turns an economic gap into a political tool.

leap.k: Income per head, Karnataka vs Bihar

secs.t: Two studies, opposite answers: who carries the GST?
secs.s: Share of total GST paid by each group, %
secs.r: Oxfam estimated in 2023 that the poorest half of Indians paid 64% of GST and the richest tenth just 3%, which would make the tax sharply regressive. A 2025 study by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, using the government’s 2022–23 consumption survey, found the bottom half paying about 30% and the top fifth about 40%, and called GST mildly progressive. The difference lies in method: how spending is split across groups and which goods are taxed at which rate. What both agree on is that GST reaches every household, however poor.
secs.src: Oxfam India, Survival of the Richest (2023), via Outlook; Sacchidananda Mukherjee, NIPFP Working Paper 430 (July 2025), via Next IAS. Groups differ: Oxfam uses top 10% and middle 40%, NIPFP top 20% and middle 30%; NIPFP figures are the average of rural and urban.

secs.t: Two of every three people who file a return pay no income tax
secs.s: Individual income-tax returns, crore, financial year 2023–24 (filed by December 2024). *2024–25 returns filed by December 2025
secs.r: Of 8.4 crore returns, 5.6 crore showed no tax due; 2.8 crore people paid. Only about 35 lakh filers owe more than ₹5 lakh a year in tax, under one in twenty. From 2025–26, incomes up to ₹12 lakh are exempt under the new regime, and at least four in five filers are expected to owe nothing. Income tax is paid by a narrow salaried and professional slice.
secs.src: Income Tax Department data via A2Z Taxcorp; PRS Legislative Research, Vital Stats: Direct Taxes in India (2025).

secs.t: Individuals now pay more income tax than companies do
secs.s: Corporate tax as % of direct tax collections; budgeted collections 2026–27, ₹ lakh crore
secs.r: In 2010–11 companies paid two-thirds of India’s direct taxes. By 2024–25 they paid under half. The 2019 cut in the base corporate rate, to 22% for firms giving up exemptions, cost an estimated ₹1.45 lakh crore a year, while personal income tax kept rising with salaries. The 2026–27 budget expects ₹14.7 lakh crore from income tax and ₹12.3 lakh crore from companies. Even among companies tax is concentrated: 743 firms, 0.1% of the total, paid 53% of corporate tax in 2022–23.
secs.src: Factly (Union Budget data); The Wire (Budget at a Glance 2026–27); PRS Vital Stats.

secs.t: The richest 1% own 40% of the wealth, and wealth itself is not taxed
secs.s: Share of national income and wealth held by the top 1%, %, 2022–23. *Revenue from a 2% tax on the 167 richest families, % of national income
secs.r: India abolished its wealth tax in 2015 and its estate duty in 1985. Gains on assets are taxed only when sold, at rates below those on salaries. The World Inequality Lab estimates a 2% annual tax on the net wealth of India’s 167 richest families would raise 0.5% of national income.
secs.src: World Inequality Lab (Chancel, Bharti, Kumar, Piketty, 2024); Oxfam India.

secs.t: GST 2.0 cut taxes on everyday goods and added a 40% rate for luxuries
secs.s: Revenue effect of the September 2025 GST rate rationalisation, ₹ thousand crore a year (estimates)
secs.r: From 22 September 2025, milk, bread and fresh produce were exempted, soaps, toothpaste and farm equipment moved to 5%, and small cars and air conditioners fell from 28% to 18%. Luxury and sin goods moved to a new 40% slab. The net revenue cost was estimated at ₹48,000 crore. Lower rates on essentials help poorer households most as a share of their spending; cheaper cars and air conditioners help the better-off.
secs.src: GST Council decisions and estimates, via Wikipedia (Goods and Services Tax 2.0).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Oxfam India; NIPFP; Income Tax Department; PRS.

23.take: India taxes spending broadly, salaries narrowly, profits less than before and wealth not at all. The burden rests on consumers and the salaried middle, while the largest fortunes face the lightest touch.
