secs.t: India’s corruption score has hovered around 40 for a decade, below the world average
secs.s: Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index, India, 2012–2025 (0 = highly corrupt, 100 = very clean). Tap or hover a point.
secs.r: The index rose from 36 to a peak of 41 in 2018–19, then slipped back to 38 in 2024 and 39 in 2025. Over the same years the economy more than doubled. Rising incomes have not, on this measure, bought a cleaner state; the world average is 42.
secs.src: Transparency International, Corruption Perceptions Index 2012–2025; 2025 results via Drishti IAS.

secs.t: Cleaner than most of South Asia, well behind China and Bhutan
secs.s: Corruption Perceptions Index score, 2025
secs.r: India ranks 91st of 182 countries, level with the Maldives. Bhutan, a far poorer country, scores 71. Bangladesh, Pakistan and Myanmar score lower than India.
secs.src: Transparency International, CPI 2025, via Drishti IAS.

secs.t: Four in ten Indians who used a public service paid a bribe; nearly half used connections
secs.s: Share of people who used a public service in the previous year and paid a bribe, or used personal connections to get it, 2020
secs.r: Transparency International’s Global Corruption Barometer for Asia found India’s bribery rate the highest of the 17 countries surveyed, and its use of personal connections the highest too. Across the region, the police were where bribes were most often paid; courts and identity offices where connections mattered most.
secs.src: Transparency International, Global Corruption Barometer Asia 2020.

secs.t: More firms meet bribe demands and see corruption as a major obstacle than a decade ago
secs.s: World Bank Enterprise Surveys: firms asked for at least one bribe, and firms naming corruption a major constraint, latest two surveys. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: Between the 2014 and 2022 surveys, the share of Indian firms facing at least one bribe request rose from 23% to 27%, and the share calling corruption a major obstacle more than doubled, to 39%. Over similar periods Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines reported falls.
secs.src: World Bank Enterprise Surveys, via World Bank WDI. Survey years differ by country (shown on tap or hover).

secs.t: Direct transfers closed some leaks; grain still goes missing on a large scale
secs.r: Paying benefits straight into Aadhaar-linked bank accounts removed duplicate and ghost beneficiaries, and the government credits it with large savings. In food, which still moves physically through ration shops, a study by the research institute ICRIER estimated that 28% of the grain supplied never reached the intended households.
secs.src: ICRIER via Moneylife; DBT estimate via Business Today and All India Radio News.

secs.t: ₹16,518 crore flowed to parties through anonymous bonds before the Supreme Court struck them down
secs.s: Electoral bonds sold, March 2018 to January 2024, and the ruling party’s share of bond income received up to 2022–23
secs.r: Electoral bonds let companies and individuals give unlimited, anonymous sums to political parties. In February 2024 the Supreme Court held the scheme unconstitutional, saying voters had a right to know who funds parties. The ruling party received about 55% of bond income declared up to 2022–23; all major parties accepted bonds.
secs.src: Association for Democratic Reforms data via ETV Bharat; Supreme Court judgment, 15 February 2024.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Business Today; ICRIER; Transparency International; World Bank Enterprise Surveys.

24.take: Technology closed some leaks, but corruption that runs through police stations, permits, ration shops and party funding has not shrunk with growth. Every rupee lost is a road unbuilt, a ration not eaten, and trust in the state spent.

leap.k: Public-service users who paid a bribe
Firms calling corruption a major obstacle

secs.t: India counts one in forty-five people as disabled; the world average is one in six
secs.s: Share of population with a disability, %
secs.r: The 2011 Census found 2.68 crore disabled people, 2.21% of the population; the 2018 national survey found 2.2%. WHO estimates 16% worldwide. The gap reflects narrow survey questions and stigma that keeps families from reporting, not a healthier population. If India matched the global rate, over 20 crore Indians would have a disability.
secs.src: Census 2011; NSS 76th round (2018) via Delhi DES report; WHO Global Report on Health Equity for Persons with Disabilities (2022).

secs.t: Half of disabled Indians can read, and one in four is in the labour force
secs.s: Persons with disabilities vs all persons, %, 2017–19
secs.r: Literacy among disabled people aged seven and above was 52%, against 78% for all Indians; among disabled women it was 40%. Fewer than a quarter of disabled adults were working or looking for work, half the national rate. The 4% quota in government jobs cannot reach people who never finished school.
secs.src: NSS 76th round (2018) via Delhi DES report; NSS 75th round (2017–18) literacy; PLFS 2018–19 labour force participation (15+, usual status).

secs.t: Children with special needs thin out sharply in the senior classes
secs.s: Enrolment of children with special needs per grade, lakh, by school stage, 2024–25 (stage total ÷ number of grades)
secs.r: Per grade, about 2.3 lakh children with special needs are enrolled in Classes 6–8 but only 0.75 lakh in Classes 11–12, a fall of two-thirds; for all children, enrolment per grade falls by about a tenth between primary and higher secondary. Three schools in four have a ramp, but only a third have a toilet a disabled child can use.
secs.src: UDISE+ 2024–25, via Education for All in India.

secs.t: Fewer than a third had the certificate that unlocks benefits
secs.s: Unique Disability ID (UDID) applications by status, lakh, 2016 to August 2025; and NSS 2018 shares
secs.r: The disability certificate and UDID card are the gateway to quotas, pensions and aids. By 2018 only 29% of disabled people had a certificate and 22% had received any government help. The UDID drive has since issued 1.25 crore cards, but 22 lakh applications were rejected and nearly 15 lakh were awaiting assessment.
secs.src: Ministry of Social Justice, Lok Sabha reply (August 2025) via The Week/PTI; NSS 76th round.

secs.t: The central pension is ₹300 a month and is open to about one disabled person in twenty
secs.s: Monthly disability pension reaching beneficiaries, ₹, central share plus state top-up, selected states
secs.r: The Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension pays ₹300 a month, last raised in 2012, and only to people with 80% or greater disability who are on the 2002 poverty list. Those rules exclude about 95% of disabled Indians. What reaches a beneficiary depends on the state: ₹300 in Bihar, ₹3,000 in Andhra Pradesh.
secs.src: IDR Online, “Where India’s disability pension scheme falls short”.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Census 2011; WHO; UDISE+; Down To Earth (Union Budget 2026–27).

25.take: India has written a modern disability law and left most disabled people outside it: uncounted, uncertified, out of school and out of work, on a pension frozen for fourteen years.

leap.k: Share of people counted as disabled
leap.n: India’s survey vs WHO global estimate

leap.k: Disabled adults in the labour force

secs.t: Secondary enrolment rose fast but still trails poorer Nepal and Kenya
secs.s: Gross enrolment in secondary school, % of the age group, 2004 → latest. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: India’s secondary enrolment rose from 53% to about 80% in twenty years, a large gain. Nepal, poorer than India, has overtaken it at 90%; Indonesia and Vietnam are near universal. UDISE+, India’s own school census, puts the secondary-level gross enrolment ratio lower, at 69% in 2024–25, and the secondary retention rate at 47%.
secs.src: UNESCO via World Bank WDI; UDISE+ 2024–25 via Careers360.

secs.t: A quarter of rural 14–18-year-olds cannot read a Class 2 text fluently
secs.s: Rural Indians aged 14–18, ASER “Beyond Basics” survey, 2023: 100 squares, one per 1%
secs.r: These are young people who have mostly completed eight years of school. One in four still cannot read a simple story meant for seven-year-olds in their own language; 57% cannot divide a three-digit number by a single digit. The learning gaps of Class 3 do not close by Class 10; they are carried into the workforce.
secs.src: ASER Centre, ASER 2023 “Beyond Basics”, via The Week / PTI.

secs.t: Dropout jumps at the secondary stage
secs.s: Annual dropout rate by school stage, %, UDISE+ 2023–24 and 2024–25
secs.r: Dropout is low in the early grades and rises sharply in Classes 9–10, when children are old enough to work or marry and schools are farther away. Rates improved in 2024–25, but total enrolment fell by 11 lakh, and analysts question how completely the database tracks children who leave.
secs.src: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ 2024–25, via Careers360.

secs.t: Eleven lakh teacher posts vacant; one lakh schools with a single teacher
secs.r: UNESCO’s 2021 report on Indian education found 19% of teaching posts vacant, most in rural areas, and over a lakh schools run by one teacher. The total number of teachers crossed one crore in 2024–25, and single-teacher schools fell slightly, but the shortage is concentrated where learning is weakest.
secs.src: UNESCO, State of the Education Report for India 2021, via Business Today; UDISE+ 2024–25.

secs.t: Weak schooling shows up later as idle youth and unemployable graduates
secs.s: Young people (15–24) not in employment, education or training, %, latest year
secs.r: About a quarter of young Indians are neither working nor studying, against about one in ten in Vietnam. Even those who do finish college face 13% unemployment. Each cohort that leaves school without basic skills will spend forty working years in low-productivity jobs; that is the real price of the learning gap.
secs.src: ILO, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: UNESCO via WDI; UDISE+ 2024–25; ASER 2023; youth literacy from UNESCO via WDI.

26.take: India built schools for every child but has not made secondary school worth staying in, or staffed it to teach. The bill arrives a decade later, in the labour market.

secs.t: India’s share of adults in work fell for fifteen years of fast growth
secs.s: Employment-to-population ratio, % of people aged 15+, 2004–2024 (ILO estimates). Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Between 2004 and 2019 the share of Indian adults with any work fell from 55% to 49%, mostly as women left the labour force. It recovered after 2020, to 53%, but largely through self-employment and unpaid work on family farms, the kind of work people take when there is nothing better. Vietnam and China keep around two-thirds or more of adults in work.
secs.src: ILO modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Only one Indian worker in four earns a regular wage or salary
secs.s: Wage and salaried workers, % of all employed, 2004 → 2024. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: The share of Indian workers on wages rose from 16% to 25% in twenty years, still the lowest in the panel apart from Nepal. In China six workers in ten draw a wage; in Vietnam nearly half. About 90% of Indian workers are in informal jobs without a contract, paid leave or social security.
secs.src: ILO modelled estimates, via WDI; ILO and Institute for Human Development, India Employment Report 2024, via Drishti IAS.

secs.t: The more education a young Indian has, the likelier they are to be unemployed
secs.s: Unemployment among people with advanced education (graduates and above), %, latest year; and youth unemployment, 15–24
secs.r: One Indian graduate in eight looking for work cannot find it, against fewer than one in twenty in Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines. Young people make up 83% of India’s unemployed, and the share of the unemployed with at least secondary education nearly doubled, from 35% in 2000 to 66% in 2022. Education raised expectations faster than the economy created jobs to meet them.
secs.src: ILO estimates via WDI; India Employment Report 2024.

secs.t: 1.26 crore applications for 35,208 railway jobs
secs.r: When good private jobs are scarce, the queue forms at the government’s door. The 2019 recruitment for non-technical railway posts drew about 1.26 crore applications, some 360 for every vacancy.
secs.src: PaGaLGuY on RRB NTPC 2019; India Employment Report 2024.

secs.t: India’s growth created jobs at a similar rate to its peers; its problem is quality and who is left out
secs.s: Average yearly growth of GDP and of employment, 2004–2024, %
secs.r: Measured simply, India’s employment grew about 1.75% a year against GDP growth of 6.4%, a ratio close to Bangladesh’s and Vietnam’s. The number of Indians in work rose from about 41 crore to 58 crore. “Jobless growth” in India is less an absence of jobs than an absence of good ones: too few wage jobs in factories and offices, too many people in farming and petty self-employment, and women left out.
secs.src: Calculated from World Bank WDI (GDP, constant prices; labour force and unemployment, ILO estimates).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: MoSPI PLFS; ILO via WDI; India Employment Report 2024.

27.take: India’s growth has created work but not enough good work: wage jobs with security for the educated young and for women. Without them, a demographic dividend turns into a queue.

leap.n: 2004 to 2019, while GDP grew more than 2.5 times

leap.k: Workers with a wage or salary

secs.t: A workforce the size of a large state, growing three times over
secs.s: Gig workers, lakh, and share of non-farm workforce, NITI Aayog estimate and projection
secs.r: NITI Aayog counted 77 lakh gig workers in 2020–21, 2.6% of the non-farm workforce, and projects 2.35 crore by 2029–30, 6.7%. India already has about a fifth of the world’s platform workers. Gig work has become a common door into urban employment for young men who cannot find salaried jobs.
secs.src: NITI Aayog, India’s Booming Gig and Platform Economy (2022), via Business Today; ILO via Outlook Business.

secs.t: Long days, thin margins
secs.s: App-based cab drivers and delivery workers, 8 cities, 2024 survey of 10,336 workers, %
secs.r: 83% of cab drivers and 75% of delivery workers worked more than ten hours a day; almost a third of cab drivers worked over fourteen. After fuel, food and vehicle costs, 43% of cab drivers took home under ₹500 a day, and a third of delivery workers under ₹10,000 a month. NCAER found food-delivery workers’ real monthly pay in 2022 was 11% below 2019. Company figures paint a better picture: Zomato reports average earnings of ₹102 an hour in 2025.
secs.src: PAIGAM and IFAT survey (March 2024), via The Quint; NCAER (2022) and Zomato (2025), via Outlook Business.

secs.t: Four in ten face violence at work, and nearly half have no insurance
secs.s: Share of gig workers, %
secs.r: Nearly half of app-cab drivers and four in ten delivery workers reported violence at work. Nearly half of gig workers have no insurance of any kind. Road accidents on delivery runs are rarely recorded as workplace injuries, and an account can be blocked by the algorithm with no hearing.
secs.src: PAIGAM and IFAT (2024); CIIE.CO survey of 4,016 gig workers (2022), via Outlook Business.

secs.t: Young, urban and schooled: the profile of a restless workforce
secs.s: Characteristics of gig workers and the labour market around them
secs.r: Two-thirds of gig workers are between 24 and 38. Most have finished middle or high school, and one in seven has a degree. They work in the same cities, wait at the same corners and share the same phone groups. Around them, youth unemployment is near 16%, and two-thirds of India’s unemployed are educated. Connected, urban and stuck: groups like this have often been at the front of street protest elsewhere.
secs.src: Assocham–Primus Partners (2021) and CIIE.CO (2022), via Outlook Business; ILO via World Bank WDI (youth unemployment, 2025); India Employment Report 2024 (ILO and IHD).

secs.t: From scattered protests to nationwide strikes
secs.s: Key events, 2023–2026
secs.r: The December 2025 strikes were the largest coordinated stoppages by delivery workers so far. They won something: in January 2026 the Labour Ministry asked quick-commerce platforms to stop promising 10-minute delivery. But participation was uneven, platforms brought in replacements and incentives, and in Bengaluru the strike fizzled. The workforce is restless but fragmented.
secs.src: GroundXero; Al Jazeera; Gulf News; Deccan Herald; Medianama.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: NITI Aayog; Zomato; PAIGAM; union statements.

28.take: A growing army of young, educated, precarious workers, controlled by apps and outside labour law, is the kind of group that turns grievance into protest. Whether it becomes a revolt depends on whether the social security now promised arrives in time.

secs.t: India has started ageing at a fraction of the income at which East Asia did
secs.s: GDP per person (constant 2015 US$) in the year the 65+ share first reached 7% of the population
secs.r: Japan began ageing as a rich country, South Korea as an upper-middle one. India reached the same point at about the income China had in 2000. China then ran two decades of 8–10% growth and still reached 14% elderly, an ‘aged society’, at about $12,500 a head, well short of high income. India would need to do better than China did.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI (SP.POP.65UP.TO.ZS, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD).

secs.t: India’s ageing has begun where China’s stood in 2000
secs.s: Population aged 65 and over, % of total, 1960–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: China went from 7% elderly in 2000 to 14% in 2023. India is on a slower but similar path: UNFPA projects the share aged 60 and over to rise from about a tenth in 2022 to 15% by 2036 and 21% by 2050, when one Indian in five will be over 60. From around 2046 there will be more elderly Indians than children.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; UNFPA India Ageing Report 2023, via Factly and Outlook.

secs.t: Fertility has fallen below replacement, fastest in the richer states and cities
secs.s: Total fertility rate, births per woman, Sample Registration System 2023
secs.r: India’s fertility is 1.9, below the 2.1 needed to replace each generation. Urban women average 1.5 children; Delhi 1.2, close to South Korea’s levels a decade ago. Only Bihar and a few northern states remain well above replacement. The south and west will age first and fastest, while the young population of the north still needs jobs.
secs.src: Registrar General of India, SRS Statistical Report 2023, via C4S.

secs.t: At past growth rates, India reaches China’s ‘aged’ income only in the 2050s
secs.s: India’s GDP per person, constant 2015 US$, at three steady growth rates of income per person, 2024–2050 (illustration)
secs.r: At 5% a year, roughly India’s pace in the last two decades, income per person would reach about $8,500 by 2050, still below what China earned when it turned ‘aged’. At 7.8% a year, the pace the World Bank says India’s whole economy needs to be high-income by 2047, it would reach about $13,500 by 2047. The elderly share will keep rising whichever line India follows.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI (2024 base); World Bank, Becoming a High-Income Economy in a Generation (2025). The World Bank’s 7.8% refers to GDP; per-person growth would be slightly lower.

secs.t: Most elderly Indians have no pension and many have no income
secs.s: India’s elderly, latest survey data
secs.r: More than 40% of India’s elderly are in the poorest fifth of households, and nearly one in five has no income of their own. Only one in four elderly men and fewer than one in twelve elderly women who worked in the organised sector draw a pension. The central old-age pension is ₹200 a month, unchanged since 2007. Women live longer, are more often widowed, and are the poorest of the old.
secs.src: UNFPA India Ageing Report 2023 via Outlook; LASI Wave 1 (2017–18) via ORF, “Old, Frail and Poor” (2025).

secs.t: The share of dependants has fallen to its lowest; from here it turns
secs.s: Dependants (under 15 and over 64) per 100 people of working age, 1960–2024
secs.r: India has never had fewer dependants per worker than today. The Economic Survey of 2018–19 projected the working-age share to peak around 2041. That gain counts only if the extra workers have jobs: with women’s workforce participation around a third and most work informal, much of the dividend is going unused.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (SP.POP.DPND); Economic Survey 2018–19 via Drishti IAS.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: World Bank WDI; UNFPA; Drishti IAS; World Bank (2025).

29.take: India has begun to age while still lower-middle income. Unless growth runs faster than ever before and puts women and the young to work now, it will be old long before it is well-off, and the old-age safety net, at ₹200 a month, is not ready.

leap.n: South Korea (2000) vs India (2024), constant 2015 US$

secs.t: Water per person crossed the stress line around 1990 and is nearing scarcity
secs.s: Internal renewable freshwater per person, cubic metres a year, 1961–2022. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Rain and rivers have not changed much; the number of people sharing them has. India fell below 1,700 m³ per person, the usual threshold of water stress, around 1990, and is now close to 1,000 m³, the threshold of scarcity. China has about twice India’s water per person; Pakistan, which depends on the Indus, has a fifth.
secs.src: FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank WDI (ER.H2O.INTR.PC). Thresholds: Falkenmark water stress index.

secs.t: Farms take nine of every ten litres India withdraws
secs.s: Agriculture’s share of annual freshwater withdrawals, %, 2022
secs.r: Industry and households share the last tenth. China has cut agriculture’s share to 62% as factories and cities grew; India’s has barely moved from 93% in 1975. Any lasting fix to India’s water runs through its fields.
secs.src: FAO AQUASTAT via World Bank WDI (ER.H2O.FWAG.ZS).

secs.t: Each cubic metre of water produces a sixth of the output it does in China
secs.s: GDP per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn, constant 2015 US$, 2022
secs.r: India earns $4.6 of GDP for every cubic metre it draws. China earns $29, Bangladesh $8.5. Low water productivity is the mirror of a farm-heavy economy that floods paddy fields with nearly free water and power.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (ER.GDP.FWTL.M3.KD).

secs.t: Three northern states pump out far more groundwater than rain puts back
secs.s: Stage of groundwater extraction: annual extraction as % of annual extractable recharge, 2025. Above 100% the aquifer is shrinking.
secs.r: Nationally, India draws 61% of its renewable groundwater, a figure that has eased slightly since 2017. The average hides the hotspots: Punjab draws 156%, Rajasthan 147% and Haryana 136%. One assessment unit in four is over-exploited, critical or semi-critical.
secs.src: CGWB and states, Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India 2025, via Rajya Sabha reply reported by ETV Bharat; Vision IAS.

secs.t: Taps reached four in five rural homes; safe, regular water reached fewer
secs.s: Jal Jeevan Mission: rural households with a tap connection, and a 2024 check of certified villages
secs.r: Rural tap coverage rose from about 17% in 2019 to 81% by mid-2025, one of the fastest piped-water roll-outs anywhere. But a government-commissioned survey of villages already certified as fully served found 83% of households got water in the previous week, 80% got the promised 55 litres a person, and only 76% of samples passed basic quality tests.
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti, Lok Sabha reply (July 2025) via IANS; IPSOS functionality assessment 2024 via SuperKalam/The Hindu.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti; CGWB; World Bank WDI; Lok Sabha replies.

30.take: India has delivered pipes faster than it has managed water. The supply is fixed, the farms take nearly all of it, and the north-west is drawing down its savings.

leap.k: Tap water that met quality tests

secs.t: Rice alone outweighs wheat; pulses and oilseeds are an afterthought
secs.s: Production, million tonnes, 2024–25 (final estimates)
secs.r: India produced a record 358 million tonnes of foodgrains in 2024–25. Rice and wheat made up three quarters of it. Pulses, the main protein for most Indians, came to 26 million tonnes, less than a fifth of the rice crop.
secs.src: Ministry of Agriculture final estimates, via Outlook Business (21 November 2025).

secs.t: Government granaries hold more than twice what the buffer requires
secs.s: Central pool stocks vs buffer norm, lakh tonnes, 1 July 2026
secs.r: On 1 July 2026 the Food Corporation held 523 lakh tonnes of wheat against a norm of 276, and 403 lakh tonnes of rice against 135, with a further 206 lakh tonnes of rice still in unmilled paddy. Storing, insuring and eventually selling off this surplus costs the exchequer every year.
secs.src: FCI data via Business Today (8 October 2026).

secs.t: Imports fill the gaps the grain-first policy leaves
secs.s: Imports, million tonnes
secs.r: Edible oil imports more than doubled in eleven years to 16.4 million tonnes, costing $20.8 billion and meeting over 60% of demand. Pulses imports hit a record 7.3 million tonnes in 2024–25, nearly three times the average of the six years before.
secs.src: SEA and trade data via Vajiram & Ravi; Ministry of Agriculture.

secs.t: The state buys mainly rice and wheat, and mostly from a few states
secs.s: Share of national production vs share of central procurement, %, 2019–20
secs.r: Minimum support prices are announced for 23 crops, but assured purchase exists almost only for paddy and wheat. Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh grow 46% of India’s wheat but supply 85% of what the government buys. In Punjab the state bought 92% of the rice crop. A farmer there has every reason to keep planting paddy.
secs.src: PRS Legislative Research, MSP and public procurement.

secs.t: India sells 38% of the world’s traded rice, and ships out its groundwater with it
secs.s: Rice exports, million tonnes, by financial year (2025–26 projected)
secs.r: Each kilogram of rice takes roughly 3,000–4,000 litres of water. Rice exports in 2018–19 carried about 24 billion cubic metres of water abroad. Much of it was pumped from aquifers in Punjab and Haryana that are already drawn at 136–156% of recharge.
secs.src: ThePrint (exports, Ashok Gulati on water use); Journal of Applied and Natural Science (2021) via Outlook Business (virtual water); CGWB 2025.

secs.t: India harvests far less grain per hectare than its neighbours
secs.s: Cereal yield, kg per hectare, latest year
secs.r: India’s cereal yield is 3.6 tonnes a hectare, close to Pakistan’s and far below China’s 6.4 or Vietnam’s 6.0. Record harvests come from planting more land and pumping more water, not from getting more out of each field.
secs.src: FAO via World Bank WDI (AG.YLD.CREL.KG); 2024 for India and Bangladesh, 2023 for others.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: FCI; Ministry of Agriculture; SEA.

31.take: India’s farm policy rewards tonnes of rice and wheat. The result is overflowing granaries, rising import bills for dal and oil, and aquifers in the grain belt running dry.

leap.k: Rice and wheat in government stores

secs.t: Two homes in three send their wastewater into open drains, soak pits or nowhere
secs.s: Where households’ wastewater goes, % of households, 2019–21
secs.r: Only 34% of Indian homes are connected to a closed drain. Another 38% let kitchen, bath and toilet water run into open drains that flow past homes and into streams. In villages, 28% of households have no drainage at all. Toilets are only one source: most household wastewater is greywater from washing and cooking, and it goes wherever the drain does.
secs.src: NFHS-5 (2019–21), analysed in Jain et al. (2024), via India Water Portal. The remainder includes soak pits and households with no drainage.

secs.t: Fewer than one litre in five of household wastewater flows into a sewer
secs.s: Domestic wastewater generated, by the system that receives it, %
secs.r: Septic tanks receive more than half of India’s domestic wastewater; sewers receive 18%. A septic tank is safe only if it is sealed and emptied into a treatment plant. Many are emptied by private tankers into fields and drains, and the overflow of many more runs into the street drain.
secs.src: WHO and UN-Habitat, SDG 6 data portal, India country profile.

secs.t: Cities generate 72,000 million litres of sewage a day and treat 20,000
secs.s: Urban sewage and treatment, million litres a day (MLD), 2020 national inventory
secs.r: Treatment plants were built for 44% of urban sewage; plants actually running could handle 37%; and the volume that reached them and was treated was 28%. The rest, about 52,000 million litres a day, went untreated into rivers, lakes, the sea and the ground. Some plants run below capacity because the sewer lines to feed them were never laid.
secs.src: CPCB national inventory of sewage treatment plants (2021), via Lok Sabha reply.

secs.t: India treats a smaller share of household wastewater than China, Vietnam or Pakistan
secs.s: Domestic wastewater flows safely treated, %, latest year (2022–24)
secs.r: India safely treats 29% of its domestic wastewater, about the South Asian average and half the world’s 56%. China and Mexico treat two-thirds. India does not report the share of industrial wastewater safely treated at all.
secs.src: WHO and UN-Habitat, SDG indicator 6.3.1, SDG 6 data portal.

secs.t: Industrial effluent is tracked river by river, not nationally
secs.s: Grossly polluting industries on the Ganga and Yamuna, and recent inspection results
secs.r: India has no published national figure for how much industrial wastewater is generated or treated. What exists is river by river: 3,186 grossly polluting industries on the Ganga and Yamuna discharge about 403 million litres of effluent a day. Inspections find most units compliant, but one in seven failed in Sonipat in 2023; the notices issued were withdrawn after later inspections found the units compliant.
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti, Lok Sabha replies (AU436; AU207, 3 February 2025; AU1613, 5 December 2024); SDG 6 data portal.

secs.t: Only one water body in ten that India monitors has good water quality
secs.s: Share of monitored water bodies with good ambient water quality, 2023; polluted river stretches
secs.r: Untreated sewage and effluent end up in the rivers and lakes that supply drinking water downstream. India reports good ambient quality in just 10% of the water bodies it monitors. The count of polluted river stretches has fallen, from 351 in 2018 to 296 in 2025, but most remain.
secs.src: SDG indicator 6.3.2 via SDG 6 data portal; CPCB polluted river stretches (2018, 2025).

secs.t: Nearly 500 workers died cleaning sewers and septic tanks since 2019
secs.s: Deaths while cleaning sewers and septic tanks, by year (2026: January–June)
secs.r: Where sewers and tanks are badly built and maintained, people are sent in to clear them by hand. Manual scavenging has been banned since 1993, yet 498 people died entering sewers and septic tanks between January 2019 and June 2026. The NAMASTE scheme has so far validated about 90,000 sanitation workers for safety gear, training and insurance.
secs.src: National Commission for Safai Karamcharis, Lok Sabha reply, via Business Standard (5 August 2026).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: CPCB; Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) via Indian Infrastructure; SDG 6 data portal.

32.take: India has toilets in almost every home, but most of what leaves those homes, and its factories, is still neither piped nor treated. Safe sewage needs closed drains, working plants and honest numbers.

leap.n: of 72,368 million litres a day, 2020 inventory

leap.k: Homes draining into a closed drain

secs.t: Officially, India’s forests are growing slowly, but most of the cover is thin
secs.s: Forest and tree cover by canopy density, % of geographical area, 2023
secs.r: The State of Forest Report 2023 counts 21.76% of India as forest cover and a further 3.41% as trees outside forests, a total of 25.17%, up 1,445 sq km since 2021. But only 3% of the country is very dense forest. ‘Forest cover’ means any patch of one hectare or more with at least 10% tree canopy, whatever the trees and whoever owns the land, so orchards, tea gardens and plantations count.
secs.src: Forest Survey of India, ISFR 2023, via ClearIAS. Tree cover share computed from 1,12,014 sq km of 32,87,263 sq km.

secs.t: India and China have added forest area; Indonesia and Brazil have lost it
secs.s: Forest area, % of land area, 1990–2023. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: On the FAO’s measure, India’s forest area rose from 21.5% of land in 1990 to 24.5% in 2023, and Vietnam’s and China’s rose faster. Indonesia and Brazil cleared tropical forest on a vast scale. India’s rise is modest, and it measures area, not the age or richness of what stands on it.
secs.src: FAO Forest Resources Assessment via World Bank WDI (AG.LND.FRST.ZS).

secs.t: Satellites show steady loss of natural forest
secs.s: Global Forest Watch estimates for India, 2001–2024
secs.r: India lost 2.31 million hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2024, 7.1% of what stood in 2000, and 348,000 hectares of humid primary forest, the oldest and most carbon-rich. Over 2000–2020 it also gained 1.78 million hectares of tree cover, including plantations. Net figures can rise while natural forest shrinks. FAO data put India second in the world for deforestation in 2015–2020, at 668,000 hectares a year.
secs.src: Global Forest Watch (University of Maryland), via Drishti IAS (June 2025); FAO.

secs.t: Three lakh hectares of forest land were handed over for projects in fifteen years
secs.s: Forest land approved for non-forest use, 2008–09 to 2022–23, thousand hectares, by purpose
secs.r: About 3.06 lakh hectares of forest land were diverted across 17,301 projects. Of the purposes itemised, mining took the most, followed by roads, irrigation and power lines. Compensatory afforestation was ‘taken up’ on over 9 lakh hectares, but how much of it survived as forest is not reported, and planting saplings elsewhere does not replace an old forest’s soil, water and wildlife.
secs.src: Ministry of Environment, Lok Sabha replies, via Factly. ‘Other uses’ covers purposes not itemised in the source.

secs.t: The most forested region is losing cover while the country gains
secs.s: Change in forest cover, sq km, 2021–2023, selected states
secs.r: The eight north-eastern states lost 327 sq km of forest cover in two years, even as India as a whole gained 156 sq km. Nagaland, Tripura and Assam lost most; Mizoram gained. Shifting cultivation, logging and road building are the main drivers, and they fall on some of India’s richest forests.
secs.src: ISFR 2023 via EastMojo; ClearIAS.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Forest Survey of India; Global Forest Watch; Ministry of Environment; Constitutional Conduct Group via The Wire.

33.take: India is planting trees and losing forests at the same time. The headline number counts green canopy; what is disappearing are old natural forests that no plantation can replace.

secs.t: The five warmest years on record all came after 2008
secs.s: India’s annual mean temperature, °C above the 1991–2020 average, warmest years since 1901
secs.r: 2024 was 0.65°C above the 1991–2020 average, beating 2016. Night-time minimum temperatures have risen slightly faster than daytime maxima, which matters for the poor: hot nights in crowded, uncooled homes deny the body its recovery.
secs.src: India Meteorological Department, via Data for India.

secs.t: Heat cost India 247 billion working hours in 2024, two-thirds of them in farming
secs.s: Potential labour hours lost to heat exposure, India, 2024: share by sector
secs.r: The Lancet Countdown estimates India lost 247 billion potential labour hours to heat in 2024, about 2.2 times the 1990s level, and $194 billion in income. Agriculture accounted for 66% of the hours and construction 20%. These are the sectors where most of India’s poorest workers earn a daily wage.
secs.src: 2025 Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change, India data sheet, via Outlook Business. Share of GDP computed against 2024 GDP of $3.9 trillion.

secs.t: Three-quarters of India’s workers labour in the heat
secs.s: Share of working hours lost to heat stress, %, ILO estimate and projection
secs.r: The World Bank estimates that 75% of India’s workforce, about 38 crore people, depend on heat-exposed labour. The ILO projected India would lose 5.8% of all working hours to heat by 2030, the equivalent of 34 million full-time jobs, over two-fifths of the global total of 80 million.
secs.src: ILO, Working on a Warmer Planet (2019), via YourStory; World Bank, Climate Investment Opportunities in India’s Cooling Sector (2022), via Business Today.

secs.t: Each extra degree cuts an informal worker’s earnings by about a seventh
secs.s: Change in net earnings (red) and coping costs (gold) of informal workers in north-west Delhi, May–June 2019, %
secs.r: A study of 396 self-employed and daily-wage workers in Delhi found that a 1°C rise in maximum temperature cut net earnings by 14%, and during heatwaves earnings fell 40%. At the same time spending on medicine, water and ice rose 14% per degree. The hotter it gets, the more the poor pay and the less they earn.
secs.src: Das and Somanathan, Delhi informal workers study, via Mongabay India (January 2025).

secs.t: One urban home in six has an air conditioner; one rural home in twenty-five does
secs.s: Households owning an air conditioner, %, 2024
secs.r: Air conditioning is the clearest line between those who can escape heat and those who cannot. Ownership is concentrated among the richest urban households; most Indians rely on fans or coolers that do little in humid heat. As temperatures rise, the comfort gap becomes a health and productivity gap.
secs.src: CLASP and Bureau of Energy Efficiency household survey 2024 (4,321 households, 20 states), via Down To Earth (May 2026); NSS Multiple Indicator Survey 2020, via Data for India.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Factly (government heat-death records); Lancet Countdown; ILO.

34.take: Heat is a tax that rises with the temperature and falls on the poorest: the farmhand, the builder and the vendor lose wages, pay more to cope, and go home to houses that do not cool.

secs.t: Neck and neck until the mid-1980s, then China pulled away
secs.s: GDP per person, constant 2015 US$, 1960–2004. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: China began reforming in 1978, India in earnest in 1991. Through the early 1980s their incomes per person were within a fifth of each other. From 1982 to 2004 China’s grew 8.8% a year and India’s 3.6%: China’s more than sextupled, while India’s roughly doubled.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD).

secs.t: China entered the race with healthier, more literate, smaller families
secs.s: India vs China, early 1980s (1981 for India’s literacy)
secs.r: Whatever else it did, the Mao era left China with a workforce that lived ten years longer and was far more often literate than India’s. A Chinese child was a third as likely to die before five. When factories arrived, China had the workers ready to staff them.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (life expectancy, under-5 mortality, adult literacy, fertility).

secs.t: China invested a far larger share of its income, every year
secs.s: Gross capital formation, % of GDP, 1960–2004
secs.r: From 1982 to 2004 China put on average 37% of its GDP into roads, plants and buildings; India put 27%. India’s rate rose to 35% only in 2004. Ten points of GDP more each year, for two decades, compounds into a different country.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS).

secs.t: China’s share of world exports rose fivefold; India’s barely moved
secs.s: Share of world merchandise exports, %, 1960–2004
secs.r: Special economic zones such as Shenzhen, opened in 1980, pulled in foreign firms that used cheap, literate labour to assemble goods for export. China went from 1.3% of world goods exports in 1982 to 6.6% in 2004. India went from 0.6% to 0.85%.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (TX.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT); world total summed over reporting countries.

secs.t: Foreign investment flowed to China a dozen times faster
secs.s: Net inflows of foreign direct investment, US$ billion, 1980–2004
secs.r: By 2004 China was receiving $68 billion a year of foreign direct investment, India $5 billion. Much of China’s came from Hong Kong and Taiwan, bringing technology, managers and export contacts along with money.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (BX.KLT.DINV.CD.WD).

secs.t: China cut extreme poverty from almost everyone to a third; India from half to under half
secs.s: Share of people living on under $3 a day (2021 PPP), %, survey years
secs.r: In 1981, 97% of Chinese lived below the line; by 2005, 33%. India started far better off, at 51% in 1983, but was still at 46% in 2004. Factory jobs in coastal China did what two decades of steady but farm-bound growth in India did not.
secs.src: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, via WDI (SI.POV.DDAY).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Conference Board (Harry Wu); Rodrik and Subramanian (2004); World Bank WDI.

35.take: India and China started the 1980s level on income. China pulled ahead by putting healthier, literate workers into factories built with high investment and foreign capital; India grew respectably but kept its workers on farms.

leap.k: China’s income per person, multiple of India’s

secs.t: China added more than four Indias
secs.s: GDP, current US$ trillion, 2004–2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s economy grew five and a half times in twenty years, to $3.9 trillion. China’s grew from $2.0 trillion to $18.7 trillion: the increase alone is more than four Indias. India has grown faster since 2021 and the ratio has slipped from its 2021 peak of 5.8, but the gap in dollars has not yet begun to close.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.MKTP.CD).

secs.t: China makes three of every ten manufactured goods; India makes three in a hundred
secs.s: Share of world manufacturing value added, %, 2004 and 2020; share of world goods exports, %, 2024
secs.r: China’s share of world manufacturing more than tripled to 29%; India’s rose from 1.6% to 2.9%. China sells 15% of the world’s goods exports, India under 2%. Factories are where farm workers in China found better-paid jobs.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (NV.IND.MANF.CD, TX.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT); world totals summed over reporting countries.

secs.t: China halved the share of its workers on farms; India cut it by a quarter
secs.s: Employment in agriculture, % of all workers, 1991–2025 (ILO modelled estimates)
secs.r: In 2004 about half of both countries’ workers were on farms. China is now at 22%, India at 42%, and India’s share rose during the pandemic as workers returned to villages. Farm work is where productivity, and pay, are lowest.
secs.src: ILO modelled estimates via World Bank WDI (SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS).

secs.t: Both countries all but ended extreme poverty, China a decade earlier
secs.s: Share of people living on under $3 a day (2021 PPP), %, survey years, 2004–2022
secs.r: This is India’s strongest result against China. Extreme poverty fell from 46% to 5.3% between 2004 and 2022, a fall similar to China’s from 2005 to 2014. China reached zero on this line by 2019.
secs.src: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, via WDI (SI.POV.DDAY).

secs.t: On health, women’s work, universities and research, the gaps are still wide
secs.s: India vs China, latest year
secs.r: A child in India is nearly five times as likely to die before five as one in China, and seven times as likely to be stunted. Six in ten Chinese women are in the labour force against three in ten Indian women. China sends three quarters of young people to college and spends four times India’s share of GDP on research.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; stunting 2020 for India, 2017 for China; R&D 2020 for India, 2023 for China.

secs.t: The average Chinese uses five times as much electricity as the average Indian
secs.s: Electricity consumption, kWh per person, 2004–2023
secs.r: Electricity use tracks factories, air conditioning and appliances. India nearly tripled its consumption per person, but China quadrupled from a higher base. India’s 2023 level is below China’s in 2004.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (EG.USE.ELEC.KH.PC).

secs.t: China cut fine-particle pollution by a third in six years; India’s fell less
secs.s: Mean annual exposure to PM2.5, µg/m³, 2004–2019 (WHO guideline: 5)
secs.r: After record smog in 2013, Beijing ordered coal plants shut, factories moved and heating switched to gas. Average exposure fell from 58 to 38 µg/m³ by 2019. India’s fell from 76 to 60 over the same years and remains among the highest in the world.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, modelled estimates (EN.ATM.PM25.MC.M3).

secs.t: India now attracts more foreign investment, is younger and is free to argue
secs.s: Net foreign direct investment inflows, US$ billion, 2004–2024; tiles show 2024–25 values
secs.r: China’s foreign investment inflows collapsed after 2021 amid trade tensions; in 2024 India received more. China has begun to age before getting rich, with one person in seven over 65 and one birth per woman. India has a younger workforce and a free press and elections, which give it a way to correct course that China lacks.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (FDI, age, fertility); Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2025.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity (2019); Arvind Subramanian (2019); World Bank WDI.

36.take: India caught up with China on extreme poverty and is catching up on growth. It has not caught up on what made China rich: healthy, educated workers, women among them, moved off farms into factories.

secs.t: India’s economy grew almost sixfold; the ten largest companies grew twelvefold
secs.s: India’s GDP vs combined market value of the world’s ten largest listed companies, US$ trillion. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: From 2004 to 2014 India gained on the giants: its output almost tripled while the top ten grew by half. Since 2014 the top ten, now mostly American technology firms riding cloud computing and AI, have grown nearly eightfold. India’s economy doubled.
secs.src: market values at 31 March 2004 and 31 December of each later year (30 June for 2026), compiled from FT Global 500 and company data via Wikipedia; India’s GDP from World Bank WDI (2004–2024) and IMF WEO April 2026 (2026).

secs.t: The single largest company is now worth more than India’s annual output
secs.s: Market value of the world’s largest listed company as % of India’s GDP in the same year
secs.r: General Electric was worth 42% of India’s GDP in 2004. Apple was worth 97% in 2024. By mid-2026 Nvidia, at $4.8 trillion, was worth 117% of India’s projected $4.15 trillion output.
secs.src: as above.

secs.t: Three companies are each worth more than India produces in a year
secs.s: Market value of the world’s ten largest listed companies at 30 June 2026, with India’s 2026 GDP, US$ trillion
secs.r: Nvidia, Alphabet and Apple each top India’s GDP. Eight of the ten are American, one Taiwanese, one South Korean. None is Indian, and none is Chinese, a change from 2009, when PetroChina headed the list.
secs.src: company market values via Wikipedia (Q2 2026); IMF WEO April 2026.

secs.t: All of India’s ten largest firms together are worth a fifth of Nvidia
secs.s: Market value, US$ trillion, mid-2026
secs.r: Reliance Industries, India’s most valuable company, is worth about $206 billion, one twenty-third of Nvidia. India’s ten largest together come to about $1 trillion. The whole Indian stock market, at $5 trillion, is roughly the value of one American chipmaker.
secs.src: PTI via Outlook Business (India top ten, 3 May 2026, converted at ₹94 per US$); BSE via Bajaj Broking (17 June 2026); Wikipedia (Nvidia, world top ten).

secs.t: Four American firms will invest more than half as much as the whole Indian economy
secs.s: Planned 2026 capital spending of Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta vs India’s total investment (gross capital formation, 2024), US$ billion
secs.r: India invests about $1.3 trillion a year across every government, company and household. Four technology companies plan $725 billion of spending in 2026, mostly on AI data centres. A firm with that budget can choose where to build, and countries compete to be chosen.
secs.src: company guidance compiled by the Financial Times, via Tom’s Hardware (30 April 2026); World Bank WDI (India gross capital formation, 32.9% of GDP in 2024).

secs.t: Against a superpower India gave ground; against single firms its rules mostly held
secs.s: Five recent tests of India’s bargaining power
secs.r: When India faced the United States, which speaks for its companies, it gave ground: it dropped the “Google tax” and accepted a trade deal that ended Russian oil purchases. When India applied its own laws to individual firms, the firms paid fines, moved data and went to court, but complied.
secs.src: Indian Express via Vision IAS (equalisation levy); TIGI and India Briefing (tariffs); Reuters via 9to5Mac (Apple); Exchange4media (WhatsApp); Business Standard (RBI and Mastercard).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: IMF; BSE; TIGI; Bloomberg via BGov.

37.take: India’s bargaining power no longer comes from size alone. It comes from its market, its factories and its rules, and those hold best when India writes the rules for firms rather than negotiating them with their governments.
