secs.t: Six problems, each costing up to five percent of GDP a year
secs.s: Estimated annual economic cost, % of GDP, latest available estimate. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: The estimates come from different studies, years and methods, and some overlap (heat and air pollution both cut working hours). They should not be added to a precise total. But the order of magnitude is clear: together these problems cost India something like a tenth of its output every year, more than the economy grows in a typical year.
secs.src: Lancet Countdown 2025 (heat); World Bank (road crashes); India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative, Lancet Planetary Health 2020 (air pollution); ORF review of studies (malnutrition, 0.8–4%); NABCONS 2022 (post-harvest loss, ₹1.53 lakh crore); ICRIER (PDS leakage, ₹69,108 crore). Rupee figures converted to % of annual GDP.

secs.t: Air pollution alone costs more than India spends on public health
secs.s: Annual cost of a problem vs annual public spending, % of GDP
secs.r: India’s governments spend about 1.3% of GDP on health. Air pollution costs 1.36% in lost output; heat costs about four times that. Money spent preventing these losses would partly pay for itself.
secs.src: as above; public health spending from National Health Accounts.

secs.t: Behind the percentages are lives
secs.s: Deaths and lost work attributed to each problem, latest year
secs.r: Air pollution was linked to 16.7 lakh deaths in 2019, nearly one death in five. Road crashes killed over 1.7 lakh people in 2023. Heat cost 247 billion working hours in 2024. Tuberculosis is projected to cost $146 billion of GDP between 2021 and 2040 if current trends hold.
secs.src: IHME/Lancet Planetary Health (air); MoRTH Road Accidents in India 2023 (roads); Lancet Countdown 2025 (heat); 2024 modelling study via Business Today (tuberculosis).

secs.t: The biggest cost is the paid work India’s women are kept out of
secs.s: GDP gain from closing the gender gap in work, and annual costs above, % of GDP
secs.r: McKinsey estimated in 2018 that if Indian women took part in paid work at the rate of the best-performing country in the region, GDP would be 18%, or $770 billion, higher by 2025. That opportunity is larger than all the costs above combined. With fewer than a third of women in the labour force, it remains mostly unclaimed.
secs.src: McKinsey Global Institute, The Power of Parity: Advancing Women’s Equality in Asia Pacific (2018), via People Matters.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: MoRTH and World Bank via PIB/Drishti; ORF; World Bank Water and Sanitation Program (2010).

38.take: India pays for its unsolved problems every year, in lost work, lost lives and lost harvests. The bill is larger than the budgets meant to fix them.

secs.t: India turns income into wires and school places better than its peers, and into nutrition, health and clean air worse
secs.s: India’s result against what its income predicts, for 14 outcomes. Each bar compares India with about 150 countries, allowing for income per person; right of centre means better than expected. Dots show Bangladesh and Vietnam. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: The pattern is the argument of the two previous parts in one picture. Where the state had to build and connect, India beat the income line: electricity, clean cooking fuel, toilets, school completion. Where it had to deliver a service every day, feed children, keep women in work or clean the air, India falls well short of countries as rich as it is. Child wasting is the extreme case: more than three times the rate India’s income predicts.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI, latest year 2015–2024 for each country; outcomes regressed on log income per person (PPP, 2021 prices) across countries with over a million people. Scale: India’s gap divided by the typical gap across countries.

secs.t: Just reaching what India’s income already predicts would transform nine outcomes
secs.s: India today against the level typical for a country with India’s income, for outcomes where India falls short. Bars scaled within each row.
secs.r: None of these requires India to become rich first. They are the levels countries at India’s present income already reach. Closing them would almost halve child stunting, cut anaemia among women by two-fifths and bring nearly ten crore more women into the labour force.
secs.src: as above. “Typical” is the value predicted by the cross-country regression at India’s income.

secs.t: Poorer countries rank higher on human development than on income; India ranks seven places lower
secs.s: Rank by income per person minus rank by Human Development Index, 2023. Positive: more wellbeing than income would suggest.
secs.r: Sri Lanka, Kyrgyzstan, Vietnam and Nepal get more health and schooling from each dollar than India. A proposed target for 2036: India’s human development rank at least equal to its income rank, closing the seven-place gap.
secs.src: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025.

secs.t: At 5% a year India reaches China’s 2018 income by 2036; at the typical pace, Indonesia’s of 2019
secs.s: India’s income per person, PPP, 2021 prices: actual 2004–2024 and two paths to 2036. Tap or hover a point.
secs.r: India’s growth since 2004 averaged 5.1% a year per person. Keeping that pace takes income to about $17,600 by 2036. Slowing to 2.1%, the median for countries that reached India’s income, would leave it at about $12,600. Either way, what citizens feel depends on the conversion rate as much as on the growth rate.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, GDP per person, PPP (constant 2021 international $); projections are simple compound growth from 2024.

secs.t: Only 3 of 24 countries at India’s income kept up 5% growth for the next fifteen years
secs.s: Average yearly growth in income per person over the 15 years after each country reached India’s 2024 income (within 10%), 1990–2009. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: China, Kazakhstan and Belarus managed it; the median was 2.1%. India has already done 5% for twenty years, but sustaining it from a higher base is rare. That is why converting growth into capability, healthier and better-taught workers, more women at work, matters: it is what keeps growth going.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI; countries with at least 5 million people in 2004.

secs.t: Six numbers for the decade
secs.r: These are proposals, anchored on what countries at India’s income already achieve, not official goals. The chapters that follow set out how: investing in people, work for the many, and cities that work.
secs.src: Targets proposed here; anchors from the calculations above, UNDP and the World Bank’s Country Economic Memorandum (2025).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Union Budget speech (2019); World Bank WDI; World Bank press release (February 2025); The Wire.

39.take: Growth is the means, not the measure. If India grows as fast in the next decade as in the last, and converts that income into wellbeing only as well as a typical country does, its citizens will live very differently by 2036.

secs.t: China and Thailand raised public health spending past 3% of GDP; India is at 1.3%
secs.s: Government health spending, % of GDP, 2004–2023, and a path for India to 2.5% by 2036. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India set itself a target of 2.5% of GDP in its National Health Policy of 2017, to be reached by 2025. On WHO’s measure it reached 1.3%. China went from 1.3% to 3.4% in two decades; Thailand, whose universal coverage scheme began in 2002, spends 3.5%. Reaching 2.5% by 2036 needs a rise of about a tenth of a percentage point of GDP each year, a pace India matched during the pandemic.
secs.src: WHO Global Health Expenditure Database, via World Bank WDI. India’s National Health Accounts, which count more spending as public, put the 2021–22 figure at 1.84%.

secs.t: Where governments pay more, families pay less at the point of care
secs.s: Government health spending, % of GDP, against out-of-pocket payments as a share of all health spending, latest year. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: Indian families still pay 44% of the country’s health bill from their own pockets, against about 31–32% in China and Indonesia. In the peer panel, countries whose governments spend more generally leave less to be paid out of pocket, the payments that push families into debt when someone falls ill.
secs.src: WHO Global Health Expenditure Database, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: A focus on early reading has started to work; the gap to Vietnam is still vast
secs.s: Class 3 children in government schools able to read a Class 2 text, and learning poverty in India and peers
secs.r: After the pandemic collapse of 2022, the share of Class 3 children in government schools who could read a simple text rose to 23%, above its 2018 level, after states made early reading and arithmetic the priority of the first grades under the NIPUN Bharat mission. Vietnam, China and Sri Lanka keep learning poverty below 20% while spending a smaller share of GDP on education than India. A target of under 30% by 2036 is ambitious but has been done.
secs.src: ASER 2018, 2022, 2024 (rural, government schools); World Bank learning poverty estimates, latest year in brackets.

secs.t: Bangladesh and Nepal cut stunting faster than India; at their pace India reaches 18% by 2036
secs.s: Children under five who are too short for their age, %, 2004–2024 (UNICEF-WHO-World Bank estimates), with a path for India to 18% by 2036. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Bangladesh and Nepal started with more stunted children than India in 2004 and now have fewer. Studies credit their gains to more schooling for mothers, sanitation, community health services and rising household incomes. India’s rate fell from 48% to 33%; cutting it to 18%, the level typical at India’s income, needs a faster fall than the last twenty years.
secs.src: Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Some Indian states are already near the target; others are twice as far
secs.s: Children under five who are stunted, by state, NFHS-5 (2019–21), %
secs.r: Puducherry, Sikkim, Kerala and Punjab already have stunting near or below 25%. Meghalaya, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Gujarat are near or above 40%. The national target is mostly a target for a handful of large northern and western states, which is where money and attention should go first.
secs.src: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, NFHS-5 state fact sheets, via PIB.

secs.t: Doubling public health spending costs about 1.2% of GDP
secs.r: At 2024 prices, India’s governments spent about ₹4.3 lakh crore on health. At 2.5% of GDP they would spend about ₹8.3 lakh crore. Spread over twelve years of growth, the extra is affordable; the hard part is that most health spending is by the states, so it has to be shared between them and the centre.
secs.src: Calculated from World Bank WDI (GDP at current prices, 2024: ₹330.7 lakh crore) and WHO government health spending share.

secs.t: Six numbers for people
secs.r: Each target is a level that some country at or below India’s income has already reached, or a goal India has set itself and missed. Each can be checked by an independent survey, if the surveys are run on time.
secs.src: Targets proposed here; anchors from WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank, NFHS and India’s National Health Policy (2017) and National Education Policy (2020).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: National Health Policy 2017; National Education Policy 2020; NIPUN Bharat guidelines (2021); WHO via WDI; ASER 2024.

40.take: India has built schools, clinics and an insurance scheme. What it has not done is spend enough, steadily enough, on what happens inside them: food for children, teaching for reading, and care that families do not pay for at the door.

leap.n: children unable to read at age 10

secs.t: Every fast-growing economy moved workers off the land; India’s move stalled and then reversed
secs.s: Share of workers in agriculture against income per person (PPP, log scale), 1991–2024. Each line is one country’s path; dots mark 1991 and 2024. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: As incomes rise, people leave farms for factories and towns. China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand all followed that path. India followed it until 2019, when the farm share reached 41%. Then it turned back: by 2024, 42% of Indian workers were again in agriculture, as the pandemic and a lack of better jobs pushed people home. Bangladesh shows the same recent reversal.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; ILO modelled employment estimates; income per person PPP, constant 2021 international $.

secs.t: India needs about 80 lakh new jobs off the farm every year
secs.r: India’s working-age population grows by more than a crore a year, and the labour force grew faster still after 2019 as more women were counted as working. The government’s own Economic Survey estimates that the economy must create about 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs a year until 2030 just to absorb the new workers.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (population aged 15–64; labour force, ILO estimates); Economic Survey 2023–24, via DT Next.

secs.t: A path back to 20%: what Bangladesh and Vietnam reached
secs.s: Manufacturing value added, % of GDP, 2004–2024, and a path for India to 20% by 2036. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Bangladesh’s factories are 22% of its economy, Vietnam’s 24%. India’s share has fallen to 12.6%. Getting to 20% in twelve years means manufacturing growing about four percentage points a year faster than the rest of the economy.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (national accounts).

secs.t: Vietnam exports fifteen times as many manufactured goods per person as India
secs.s: Manufactured goods exported per person, US$, latest year
secs.r: The economies that built factory jobs at scale did it by selling to the world: garments in Bangladesh, electronics in Vietnam, almost everything in China. India sells about $200 of manufactured goods per person a year; Vietnam sells about $3,000. Export markets are large enough to employ millions without waiting for Indian demand to grow.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI (merchandise exports, manufactures share, population). Bangladesh: 2018, latest available.

secs.t: A path to 45%: what Indonesia already has
secs.s: Women’s labour-force participation, ILO estimates, % of women aged 15+, 2004–2024, and a path for India to 45% by 2036. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Indonesia has 54% of its women in the labour force and Vietnam 69%. A target of 45% for India by 2036 is roughly the World Bank’s path to 50% by 2047. It needs jobs women can reach: factories and offices near home, safe transport, childcare, and hostels for women who migrate for work, as electronics plants in Tamil Nadu that house women workers in hostels have begun to show.
secs.src: ILO modelled estimates, via World Bank WDI; World Bank Country Economic Memorandum (2025).

secs.t: Five numbers for work
secs.r: These targets do not ask India to copy China. Each has already been reached by Bangladesh, Vietnam or Indonesia, all poorer than China.
secs.src: Targets proposed here; anchors from World Bank WDI and the World Bank’s Country Economic Memorandum (2025).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Make in India (2014); Ministry of Labour notification (November 2025), via K&S Partners; World Bank (February 2025); ILO via WDI.

41.take: Growth that does not create work for farm labourers and women leaves most Indians watching it. Factory jobs built for export, and the conditions that let women take them, are how growth reaches the many.

secs.t: Three targets for a state that maintains what it builds
secs.s: Today, and the proposed 2036 target, for road deaths, air and sewage
secs.r: All three are failures of running things rather than building them: enforcing speed limits and helmet rules, controlling burning and dust, operating sewage plants and connecting homes to them. The targets are anchored on international benchmarks: the UN goal of halving road deaths, WHO’s first interim air-quality target, and treating most of the sewage cities already produce.
secs.src: MoRTH (2024); IQAir (2025); CPCB (2021); targets proposed here.

secs.t: India’s towns added 19 crore people in twenty years, and will add many more
secs.s: Urban share of the population, %, 2004–2024 (national definitions). Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s urban population rose from 33 crore to 51 crore between 2004 and 2024, yet by official definitions only 35% of Indians are urban, far fewer than in China or Indonesia. Many places that look and function like towns are still governed as villages. As the share rises, the cost of not running cities well rises with it.
secs.src: UN World Urbanization Prospects, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Brazil’s cities raise seven times as much as India’s, relative to the economy
secs.s: Municipal revenue, % of GDP
secs.r: Indian municipalities raise and spend about 1% of GDP, a share that has not grown in more than a decade. Brazil’s raise 7.4% and South Africa’s about 6%. The 74th Amendment of 1992 gave cities eighteen functions, from water supply to urban planning; most were never matched with money or staff. Cities that cannot collect property tax cannot pay for sewers, footpaths or traffic police.
secs.src: Reserve Bank of India, Report on Municipal Finances (2022), via Drishti IAS.

secs.t: Halving road deaths by 2036 means reversing a twenty-year climb
secs.s: Road deaths reported by police, 2004–2024, and a path to half the 2024 level by 2036. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Ten countries, among them Japan, Norway and the UAE, more than halved road deaths between 2010 and 2021. Their tools are known: speed cameras and enforced limits, helmet and seat-belt checks, safe crossings and footpaths, and ambulances that reach the injured within the hour. Two-thirds of India’s road dead are on two wheels or on foot; that is where the first gains lie.
secs.src: MoRTH; WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023, via Deccan Herald.

secs.t: Pedestrians die where streets have no room for them
secs.r: One in five people killed on Indian roads is a pedestrian; in Mumbai it is nearly half. Even in cities with pedestrian policies, footpaths are missing, broken or occupied. A footpath on every arterial road is a cheap, visible target that a city council can be held to.
secs.src: MoRTH 2024, via ETV Bharat; Pune Municipal Corporation and city data compiled by Question of Cities.

secs.t: Treating 70% of urban sewage means two and a half times today’s treatment
secs.s: Urban sewage, million litres a day: generated, treated today, and treated at 70%
secs.r: India built plants for 44% of its urban sewage but treats 28%. The quickest gains are in running existing plants fully and connecting homes to them; Delhi has plants for nearly all its sewage but treats only 56% of it to standard. New capacity is needed too: about 30,000 million litres a day more treated to reach 70% at today’s sewage volumes.
secs.src: CPCB (2021), via Down To Earth; Ministry of Jal Shakti (2025), via The Week.

secs.t: Six numbers for cities
secs.r: Each target can be measured independently: road deaths by hospital and WHO estimates as well as police records, air by public monitors, sewage by river-quality tests, footpaths by a walk down the street.
secs.src: Targets proposed here; anchors from the UN road-safety goal, WHO air-quality guidelines and RBI.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992; RBI (2022); CREA (2026); MoRTH.

42.take: India built at record pace. Cities that work need a state that maintains: money and powers for city governments, enforcement on roads, and plants that actually run.

secs.t: On what citizens actually live with, India ranks 16 places below its income
secs.s: A simple index of eight everyday outcomes (0–100) against income per person, 137 countries, latest data. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: The index averages eight things a citizen feels directly: a long life, children who survive and grow, clean air, safe water, safe roads, women able to work, and power at home. India ranks 94th of 137 on it, against 78th on income. Kenya, Nepal and Ghana, all poorer, score higher; so does Bangladesh at a similar income. A published index of this kind, every year, would show voters whether growth is reaching them.
secs.src: Calculated from World Bank WDI and WHO estimates, latest year 2015–2024 for each measure; each scaled 0–100 across countries with over a million people and averaged with equal weights. An illustration of the method, not an official index.

secs.t: India scores well on power at home and roads per person; poorly on children’s growth, air and women’s work
secs.s: Scores on the eight measures (0–100), India and peers. Darker is better. Tap or hover a cell.
secs.r: The grid separates what India has fixed from what it has not. Electricity is near universal. Children’s height, clean air, safe water and women’s work are where India scores among the lowest in the panel, the same gaps the earlier chapters found one by one.
secs.src: As above.

secs.t: India’s statisticians are capable; the institutions around them are weak
secs.s: World Bank Statistical Performance Indicators, 2023: score by pillar (0–100)
secs.r: On the World Bank’s measures, India’s data production and use score well, above China and close to Indonesia. Its weakest pillar is data infrastructure: legislation, governance, standards and funding, where India scores 50 against 70 for Indonesia and Bangladesh and 85 for Mexico. The National Statistical Commission, set up in 2006, still has no statutory basis.
secs.src: World Bank Statistical Performance Indicators, via WDI. Pillars: data use, data services, data products, data sources, data infrastructure.

secs.t: Several of India’s key numbers are five to seventeen years old
secs.s: Years since the latest national measurement, as of 2026
secs.r: India’s quarterly GDP figures are a day old by comparison. The numbers that describe citizens’ lives, how many people there are, how many are poor, how many children can read, how sewage and roads are faring, are years old, and several are produced only once and then not repeated.
secs.src: Registrar General of India; MoSPI; NFHS; World Bank learning poverty; CPCB; WHO; OECD PISA.

secs.t: What honest numbers would need
secs.r: None of these is novel. Many democracies give their statistics offices legal independence and publish release calendars in advance. India’s own Rangarajan Commission recommended a statutory statistics body in 2001.
secs.src: Proposals; Rangarajan Commission on Statistics (2001); World Bank SPI.

secs.t: Sixteen numbers voters can check
secs.s: Proposed targets from the five chapters of Part VII: today’s value, the 2036 target, and how far today’s value is along the way.
secs.src: Targets proposed here, anchored on peers, WHO and UN benchmarks, and India’s own past commitments. Bars show how far India has moved since 2004 towards each target, where a comparable 2004 figure exists; red means it has moved away.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: IndiaSpend / iSignal interview with P C Mohanan; Business Standard (2019); World Bank SPI.

43.take: A democracy keeps score. India measures its economy precisely and its citizens’ lives rarely; reversing that, with independent statistics and a yearly report on what citizens feel, is the reform that makes every other target checkable.

secs.t: From 12th to 5th, with two stumbles on the way
secs.s: Rank among the world’s economies by GDP in current US dollars, 2004–2024. Hover or tap a line.
secs.r: India slipped to 14th in 2006, when commodity exporters boomed, and lost ground again in the 2012–13 rupee slide. The biggest jump came in 2015, from 10th to 7th, as oil prices collapsed and shrank Russia, Brazil and Canada in dollar terms. The top of the table is now crowded. Germany, Japan, India and Britain all sit near $4 trillion, so small currency moves reorder them.
secs.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators, May 2026 release.

secs.t: India’s slice of world output more than doubled
secs.s: India’s GDP as a share of world GDP, current US dollars
secs.r: One dollar in every 62 earned on the planet was earned in India in 2004. By 2024 it was one in 28.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; world total is the sum of countries reporting.

secs.t: Two decades, two governments, almost the same pace
secs.s: Real GDP growth by calendar year, with each decade’s average. Dots mark turning points; tap or hover for detail.
secs.r: Growth averaged 6.8% a year in 2004–13 and 6.2% in 2014–24. Leave out the pandemic year and the decades are almost identical. Each had one shock and several years above 8%.
secs.src: World Bank WDI. Calendar years; India’s official accounts use April–March fiscal years.

secs.t: “Five times larger” depends on the ruler
secs.s: Growth since 2004 on four measures (2004 = 1)
secs.r: In rupees the economy is ten times larger, mostly because prices tripled. In dollars it is 5.5 times larger. In real output, the measure of how much more India actually produces, it is 3.4 times larger. Per person the gain is 2.7 times, because 315 million people were added along the way. That is the number a household feels.
secs.src: World Bank WDI. Real output and real income per person in constant 2021 international dollars (PPP).

secs.s: Economy in 2024 as a multiple of its 2004 size
secs.r: Dollar comparisons flatter countries whose currencies held up or whose prices rose fast. Strip those effects out and India’s economy grew 3.4 times, second only to China among the peer panel and ahead of Vietnam and Bangladesh. The peer panel is the eight countries closest to India’s development profile in 2004, plus Vietnam, China and three neighbours, with the United States as a yardstick.
secs.src: World Bank WDI. Real output is GDP at constant 2021 international dollars.

secs.t: Sixth fastest of 105 countries in income growth per person
secs.s: Average yearly growth in real income per person, 2004–2024, countries with 5 million+ people. Each dot is a country; tap or hover for names.
secs.r: India’s 5.1% a year places it in a small leading group with China, Ethiopia, Cambodia, Azerbaijan, Bangladesh and Vietnam. Most of the world grew at 1–3%.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; GDP per person at constant 2021 international dollars.

secs.t: Farms still hold 42% of jobs but make 16% of output
secs.s: Each sector’s share of output and of jobs, 2004–2024
secs.r: Fourteen points of the workforce left agriculture. They went mostly into construction and informal services, not into factories. Industry’s share of output fell from 29% to 25%. Services produce half of output but employ a third of workers. That is the opposite of the farm-to-factory route that lifted China, Vietnam and Bangladesh.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; jobs are ILO modelled estimates. Output shares exclude net taxes on products.

secs.t: Steadier prices and a deep cushion of reserves
secs.s: Four indicators, 2004–2024
secs.r: Inflation averaged 8.0% in 2004–13 and 5.1% in 2014–24, helped by an inflation target adopted in 2016. Reserves rose almost fivefold, which is why a rupee that fell from ₹45 to ₹84 per dollar never turned into a 1991-style crisis. Investment peaked at 42% of GDP in 2007 and has not returned there.
secs.src: World Bank WDI. Reserves include gold; inflation is consumer prices.

secs.t: Four numbers that depend on who is counting
secs.src: government announcement (Jan 2026); IMF World Economic Outlook (Apr 2026) and February 2026 GDP base revision, as reported by The Indian Express; DPIIT gross FDI for FY2024–25; World Bank net FDI for calendar 2024; Arvind Subramanian, Harvard CID (2019).

secs.t: Fifth by the size of its economy, 143rd by the income of its people
secs.s: The ten largest economies in 2024: rank by total GDP and rank by GDP per person, among 191 countries
secs.r: No other large economy shows a gap like India’s. China ranks 79th per person and Brazil 88th. India, at $2,695 a head, sits beside Bangladesh and Cambodia.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, GDP and GDP per person in current US dollars, 2024.

01.take: The economy produces 3.4 times what it did in 2004. The average Indian earns 2.7 times as much.

secs.t: Every measure of poverty points the same way
secs.s: Share of Indians counted as poor on four measures. Tap or hover any point; the shaded years had no published consumption survey.
secs.r: Two measures count money, two count living conditions such as schooling, nutrition, cooking fuel, sanitation and housing. They were built by different bodies, Indian and international, and disagree on levels. None disagrees on direction.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (May 2026); Planning Commission via WDI; UNDP/OPHI Global MPI 2023; NITI Aayog MPI 2023 and 2024.

secs.t: Hundreds of millions left poverty on every count
secs.s: Reduction in the number of poor people, by measure and period
secs.r: The periods differ, so the bars cannot be added. Each is a separate witness. The largest, the UN’s 415 million over fifteen years, is the biggest fall in poverty recorded anywhere in that time.
secs.src: Planning Commission (2013); World Bank poverty update (June 2025); UNDP/OPHI Global MPI 2023; NITI Aayog MPI discussion paper (January 2024).

secs.t: Both decades cut poverty fast
secs.s: Fall in the poverty rate, percentage points a year, by measure and period
secs.r: In points, poverty fell slightly faster in the first decade, when there was more of it to cut. As a share of what remained, it fell faster in the second: extreme poverty shrank about 7% a year in 2004–11 and about 14% a year in 2011–22. Neither government owns the whole achievement.
secs.src: Author’s calculations from the sources above. Survey years rounded to the first calendar year.

secs.t: Eleven years without an official poverty count
secs.s: India’s national consumption surveys, the basis of every money-based poverty estimate
secs.r: The 2017–18 survey was completed and approved for release in June 2019, then withheld in November 2019 over “data quality issues”. A reported draft showed real spending per person down 3.7% since 2011–12, which would have been the first fall in more than forty years. The 2022–23 survey used a new design. It is widely judged better, but comparison with 2011–12 is imperfect.
secs.src: Ministry of Statistics announcement, 15 November 2019, and Business Standard report of the draft, via Business Today; MoSPI HCES press notes.

secs.t: A city dweller spends 70% more than a villager
secs.s: Average monthly spending per person, current rupees, and the spread of spending (Gini index), latest two surveys
secs.r: Measured spending grew 9% in villages and 8% in cities in a single year, and became more evenly spread. Surveys miss most of the very rich, so they show less inequality than income and tax records do.
secs.src: MoSPI, Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023–24 press note, December 2024. Excludes the value of free items from welfare schemes.

secs.t: Out of destitution, not yet out of poverty
secs.s: Share of Indians below three World Bank poverty lines (2021 prices)
secs.r: The fall at $4.20, from 74.5% to 23.9%, is even larger than at the extreme line. But the $8.30 line, typical of countries like Indonesia or Brazil, barely moved until the last decade. In 2022, 82.1% of Indians still lived below it.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (May 2026). Survey years 2004, 2009, 2011 and 2022.

secs.t: Of every 100 Indians, 82 live below $8.30 a day
secs.s: India’s population in 2022 by daily consumption band, each square one percent
secs.r: Most of the people who left extreme poverty are still close to it. A failed harvest, a hospital bill or a lost job can push them back.
secs.src: World Bank WDI shares applied to a 2022 population of 1.425 billion. Bands rounded to whole percentages.

secs.s: Share of people below the selected line, latest survey year (in brackets)
secs.src: World Bank WDI (May 2026). Survey years differ by country.

secs.t: Growth did most of the work; the state put a floor underneath
secs.s: Policies that bear directly on poverty, 2004–2026. Tap or hover a marker.
secs.r: Income per person rose 2.7 times and farm jobs fell from 56% to 42% of all work. On top of that came a rural jobs guarantee, subsidised and then free grain, bank accounts and basic services. Free rations for about 80 crore people are a welfare achievement, and a measure of how many Indians still cannot be left to feed themselves.
secs.src: National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005; National Food Security Act 2013; PMGKAY extension (Outlook Business, November 2023); World Bank WDI.

secs.t: How poor is India now? It depends on the method
secs.src: Bhalla, Virmani and Bhasin, IMF Working Paper (April 2022); World Bank estimate for 2019 (April 2022), as reported by Scroll; World Bank poverty update (June 2025); World Inequality Lab (March 2024); World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Fewer poor, but 102nd of 123 on hunger
secs.s: Global Hunger Index 2025 rank, South Asia (lower is better)
secs.r: Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh all rank well ahead of India. About one child in five under five is wasted, too thin for their height, a share that has barely moved across three national health surveys.
secs.src: Global Hunger Index 2025; NFHS-5 (2019–21).

02.take: Fewer than one Indian in twenty is destitute. More than four in five live below the poverty line of an upper-middle-income country.

secs.t: India cut child deaths by two-thirds and passed Bangladesh
secs.s: Under-5 deaths per 1,000 live births, India and the peer panel. Tap or hover a line to pick out a country.
secs.r: India started the period behind Bangladesh, Nepal and Indonesia. It finished ahead of Bangladesh, level with Nepal, and still behind Indonesia, Sri Lanka, China and Vietnam. China and Vietnam were already at India’s current rate in 2004.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation), May 2026 release.

secs.t: About 15 million children alive who would have died at 2004 rates
secs.s: Children dying before age five each year, India. The shaded band shows deaths that would have occurred had the 2004 rate held.
secs.r: Annual under-5 deaths fell from 2.2 million to about 615,000. Fewer births explain part of that. The rest is survival: applying 2004 death rates to the children actually born from 2005 to 2024 gives about 15 million more deaths than occurred.
secs.src: World Bank WDI; deaths avoided are the author’s estimate from births (crude birth rate × population) and the change in under-5 mortality.

secs.t: Nearly two of every three child deaths now happen in the first month
secs.s: Under-5 deaths per 1,000 births, split by age at death
secs.r: Deaths after the first year fell by 83%, the gain from vaccines, clean water and oral rehydration. Deaths in the first month fell by 57%. The remaining deaths need neonatal care units, skilled birth attendants and warm, clean delivery rooms: harder and costlier to build.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (UN IGME). Neonatal, infant and under-5 mortality rates.

secs.t: Births moved into hospitals and maternal deaths fell by three-quarters
secs.s: Hospital and clinic births (national surveys) and maternal deaths per 100,000 live births
secs.r: Nine in ten births now happen in a health facility, up from fewer than four in ten in 2005–06. Cash payments to mothers who give birth in a facility, launched in 2005, helped drive the shift. Maternal deaths fell from 296 to 80 per 100,000 births, with a sharp pandemic spike in 2021.
secs.src: National Family Health Surveys 3, 4 and 5; World Bank WDI (UN Maternal Mortality Estimation Inter-agency Group).

secs.t: Vaccine coverage rose from under two-thirds to near-universal
secs.s: Share of children aged 12–23 months vaccinated, India
secs.r: Coverage climbed steadily through both decades, dipped in the pandemic, and reached 94% and 97% by 2024. A catch-up drive from 2014 targeted districts where children had been missed.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO/UNICEF estimates of national immunisation coverage).

secs.s: 2004 (open dot) and latest (filled dot). Lower is better.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (UN IGME and MMEIG estimates). Child deaths per 1,000 births, 2004–2024; maternal deaths per 100,000 births, 2004–2023.

secs.t: Eight more years of life, but Bangladesh still lives longer
secs.s: Life expectancy at birth, years. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: Indians born in 2024 can expect to live to 72, up from 64.5. The pandemic took more than three years off in 2021, the deepest fall among the peer panel, before a full recovery. Bangladesh, level with India in 2004, now lives 2.7 years longer.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (UN World Population Prospects).

secs.t: A rural health mission, cash for safe births, a vaccine drive
secs.s: Programmes behind the fall in child and maternal deaths. Tap or hover a marker.
secs.r: Most of these programmes rebuilt the public primary-health system that poor families use. Falling poverty, more educated mothers, toilets and clean cooking fuel helped from outside the health system.
secs.src: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare programme launches.

secs.t: Where the counts agree, and where they do not
secs.src: Sample Registration System bulletins; World Bank WDI (UN estimates); WHO global excess-mortality estimates (May 2022); NFHS-5; WHO modelled anaemia estimates via WDI.

secs.t: Government still spends just 1.3% of GDP on health
secs.s: Health spending as a share of GDP: government and total, latest year (2023). Tap or tap or hover for the out-of-pocket share.
secs.r: India’s government spends 1.3% of GDP on health, against 3.4% in China and Morocco and 2.0% in Vietnam and Kenya. Out-of-pocket payments have fallen from 72% to 44% of all health spending, yet total health spending shrank as a share of the economy.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (WHO Global Health Expenditure Database).

03.take: Two-thirds fewer children die before five. The deaths that remain happen in the first month of life, where care costs most.

secs.t: From one in fifty online to seven in ten
secs.s: Share of people using the internet, India, the world and the peer panel. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India took ten years to reach 13% and then nearly quintupled that in the next decade. It has almost closed the gap with the world average, 70% against 74% in 2025, and is now ahead of every South Asian neighbour.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (International Telecommunication Union), May 2026 release.

secs.t: Data became 97% cheaper and use rose 300 times
secs.s: Average cost of 1 GB of mobile data (rupees, log scale) and data used per subscriber per month
secs.r: The fall came in one burst. A new operator launched free 4G in September 2016, and within three years the price of a gigabyte had fallen from ₹76 to under ₹9. Monthly use per subscriber went from 62 megabytes in 2014 to 18 gigabytes in 2023.
secs.src: TRAI data via FactChecker (2014–2021) and Ministry of Communications (June 2024); Department of Economic Affairs monthly review (consumption).

secs.t: India skipped the fixed line and went straight to the phone
secs.s: Subscriptions per 100 people, India
secs.r: Mobile subscriptions rose from under 5 to about 80 per 100 people. Fixed broadband never took off: about 3 lines per 100 people in 2024. Almost all of India’s internet runs over mobile networks, which serve video and payments well and long working hours less well.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (ITU). Mobile subscriptions dipped after 2019 as users dropped second SIM cards.

secs.t: Internet subscriptions nearly quadrupled in ten years
secs.s: Internet and broadband subscriptions, crore (10 million)
secs.r: Subscriptions count connections, not people. One person may hold two. Even so, the scale is vast: about 97 crore internet subscriptions in mid-2024 and 100 crore broadband connections by November 2025.
secs.src: Ministry of Communications via All India Radio (December 2024); TRAI via TelecomTalk (November 2025).

secs.t: Ahead of South Asia, behind East Asia and Morocco
secs.s: Share of people using the internet, latest year
secs.r: China and Morocco are above 90%, Vietnam 84%. Ghana and Indonesia are level with India. Every South Asian neighbour is behind.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (ITU). Latest year is 2024 or 2025 except Myanmar (2020).

secs.t: Women are 14 points behind men online, a wider gap than in any East Asian peer
secs.s: Share of women and men using the internet, latest year. Tap or tap or hover for detail.
secs.r: In India 63% of women and 77% of men are online. Bangladesh’s gap is 7 points, Indonesia’s 6, Vietnam’s 4 and China’s almost none. The gap has widened from 10 points in 2018, because men came online faster than women.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (ITU), latest year per country; India 2025.

secs.t: The world’s second-largest exporter of computer services
secs.s: Computer, communications and IT service exports, US$ billion. India over time and the top ten exporters in 2023.
secs.r: India’s software and IT service exports grew more than tenfold, to $178 billion in 2024. Only Ireland, home to the European headquarters of American tech firms, exports more.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, ICT service exports (balance of payments, current US$).

secs.t: The democracy that shuts down the internet most often
secs.s: Internet shutdowns ordered in India each year, as counted by Access Now
secs.r: India led the world in shutdowns for six straight years until 2024, when Myanmar, under military rule, ordered 85 to India’s 84. Manipur, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir account for most. A connected country is also one where the state has learned to disconnect it.
secs.src: Access Now, #KeepItOn annual reports, via Sabrang India and The Wire (2024 figures).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: World Bank WDI; FactChecker, review of a Coal Ministry claim; TRAI.

04.take: Seven in ten Indians are online, on some of the world’s cheapest data. The gap that remains is between women and men, and between connection and capability.

leap.k: Price of 1 GB of mobile data

secs.t: Reserves grew more than fivefold
secs.s: India’s foreign-exchange reserves at year end, including gold. Switch to see India’s rank among reserve holders.
secs.r: Reserves stalled at about $300 billion from 2010 to 2013 and India fell to tenth among holders. The climb resumed after 2014. Reserves fell by $71 billion in 2022 as the central bank sold dollars to defend the rupee; they were rebuilt to a record $728 billion in February 2026.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (IMF), total reserves including gold, 2004–2024; Reserve Bank of India weekly data via All India Radio (February 2026 record).

secs.t: Fifth-largest reserve holder in the world
secs.s: Total reserves including gold, 2024, US$ billion. Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Only China, Japan, the United States and Switzerland hold more. India holds more than Russia, Saudi Arabia or South Korea, and about four times as much as Indonesia or Turkey.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, 2024. Taiwan, which the World Bank does not cover, also holds about $580 billion.

secs.t: A bigger pile, but fewer months of imports
secs.s: Reserves measured as months of imports they could pay for, 2004 and 2024
secs.r: Imports grew faster than reserves. In 2004 the reserves could pay for 11 months of imports; in 2024, seven and a half. That is still more cover than almost every peer: only China, Nepal and Brazil have more, and Vietnam, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Ghana have under three months.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, total reserves in months of imports.

secs.t: From sixteenth to fourth among the world’s stock markets
secs.s: Value of listed domestic companies, US$ trillion, India. Switch to see the world rank.
secs.r: The market crashed by 60% in 2008 and recovered. Its value rose twelvefold over twenty years, to $5.1 trillion in 2024, and it passed Hong Kong in January 2024 to become the fourth largest. By mid-2026 Hong Kong had moved back ahead, leaving India fifth at about $5 trillion.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (World Federation of Exchanges); 2018 omitted because the reported value is inconsistent with adjacent years. Rank among countries the World Bank covers. Angel One (June 2026) for the mid-2026 position.

secs.t: The largest emerging stock market after China
secs.s: Value of listed domestic companies, 2024, US$ billion
secs.r: India’s listed companies are worth five times South Africa’s and nearly eight times Brazil’s. China’s are worth more than twice India’s.
secs.src: World Bank WDI. Mexico 2023.

secs.t: Foreign money arrives in record amounts, and most of it leaves again
secs.s: Net foreign direct investment into India by calendar year, and the 2025–26 flows
secs.r: Inflows peaked at $64 billion in 2020 and fell to $27 billion by 2024. In 2025–26 foreign companies brought in a record $95 billion, but they also took $54 billion home and Indian companies invested $33 billion abroad. Net, under $8 billion stayed.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (balance of payments, net inflows); Reserve Bank of India data via SuperKalam (May 2026).

secs.t: The rupee lost nearly half its dollar value; the credit rating rose for the first time in 18 years
secs.r: The rupee went from 45 to 84 to the dollar between 2004 and 2024. Prices in India rose 2.2 times as much as in the United States over those years, so adjusted for inflation the rupee actually gained strength. In August 2025 S&P raised India’s rating from BBB− to BBB, its first upgrade since 2007.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, official exchange rate (annual average) and consumer prices; S&P Global Ratings.

secs.t: Seven milestones and three setbacks in space
secs.s: Selected Indian space missions since 2004
secs.r: India became the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to land near its south pole, at a fraction of what others spent. Failures are part of the record too: two launches of the workhorse PSLV rocket failed within eight months, and the first uncrewed test of the human spaceflight programme has slipped six years.
secs.src: ISRO; Al Jazeera (PSLV-C61, May 2025); SuperKalam (PSLV-C62, January 2026); Wikipedia, Gaganyaan-1 (status as of June 2026).

secs.t: Defence exports grew 56 times in twelve years
secs.s: Defence exports, ₹ crore, financial years
secs.r: Private firms now sell more than state-owned ones: ₹15,233 crore of the ₹23,622 crore in 2024–25. The total is still small beside the large importers; ₹38,424 crore is about $4.5 billion.
secs.src: Press Information Bureau (2013–14, 2023–24, 2024–25); Ministry of Defence via Outlook Business (2025–26).

secs.t: 61 unicorns at home, 156 more founded by Indians abroad
secs.s: Start-ups valued at $1 billion or more with at least one Indian co-founder, 2026. One square per company.
secs.r: India has the fourth-largest number of unicorns in the world. More than two-thirds of the unicorns Indians have co-founded are based outside India.
secs.src: Hurun Global Unicorn Index 2026 via IANS (June 2026).

secs.t: Four numbers that need a second look
secs.src: RBI; World Bank WDI; Business Standard and Angel One; Wikipedia, Gaganyaan-1.

05.take: India now carries weight in global money: the fifth-largest reserves, a top-five stock market and a moon landing. Much of the investment that arrives does not stay.

leap.n: End-2004 to the record of February 2026

secs.t: From 1.8 crore payments a year to 2,400 crore a month
secs.s: Payments made over UPI each financial year. Switch between the number of payments and their value.
secs.r: The number of payments rose about 13,000 times in nine years. The note ban of November 2016 pushed people off cash, and the lockdowns of 2020 pushed shops onto QR codes. In August 2026 UPI carried a record 2,451 crore payments worth ₹29.8 lakh crore, about 790 million on an average day.
secs.src: NPCI annual volumes via Department of Financial Services and press reports; FY 2025–26 from the government’s reply in the Lok Sabha via YourStory and Outlook Money; August 2026 from NPCI via DT Next.

secs.t: Four layers, each built on the one below
secs.s: India’s public digital infrastructure and its reach, latest figures
secs.r: Each layer made the next one cheap. A verified ID allowed a no-frills bank account to be opened in minutes; the account and the phone made instant payments possible; and all three let the state pay welfare straight into the account instead of through officials.
secs.src: Wikipedia (Aadhaar, October 2024); UIDAI via The Tribune (May 2025); Policy Edge (Jan Dhan, August 2026); NPCI (August 2026); New India Samachar, PIB (DBT, August 2026).

secs.t: India makes about half of the world’s real-time payments
secs.s: Share of global real-time payment transactions, 2023. One square = 1%.
secs.r: Brazil’s Pix, China’s systems and the rest of the world together make up the other half. The IMF named UPI the largest retail fast-payment system in the world by volume.
secs.src: ACI Worldwide, Prime Time for Real-Time 2024, via Ministry of Finance and Business Standard (December 2025).

secs.t: Account ownership leapt from below the world average to above it
secs.s: Adults with an account at a bank or mobile-money provider. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India went from 35% in 2011 to 89% in 2024, ten points above the world average. The biggest jump, 27 points, came between 2014 and 2017, the first three years of Jan Dhan. Only China and Kenya in the peer panel are level.
secs.src: World Bank Global Findex, via World Development Indicators. Survey years 2011, 2014, 2017, 2021 and 2024 (Vietnam 2022).

secs.t: The poorest and women were reached too
secs.s: Account ownership among women and men in India, and among the poorest 40% across the peer panel
secs.r: In 2011 men were 17 points more likely than women to have an account; by 2024 the gap had gone. Among the poorest 40% of adults, 86% have an account, more than in China and far more than in Bangladesh, Pakistan or Indonesia. In Pakistan only 12% of women do.
secs.src: World Bank Global Findex, via WDI.

secs.t: 59 crore no-frills accounts, one in four lying idle
secs.s: Jan Dhan accounts, crore
secs.r: Accounts quadrupled from 14.7 crore in March 2015 to 59.1 crore in August 2026, and deposits grew twentyfold to ₹3.17 lakh crore. Average balance is about ₹5,356. But 15.4 crore accounts are inoperative and 5.7 crore hold nothing.
secs.src: Policy Edge, from Ministry of Finance data (August 2026); Department of Financial Services reply to an RTI application, via Free Press Journal (12 August 2026 data).

secs.t: Indians are four times as likely as others to leave an account unused
secs.s: Account owners with no deposit or withdrawal in the past year, 2024
secs.r: One in six Indian account owners neither paid in nor took out money in a year, against one in twenty-five across low- and middle-income countries. Women’s accounts are idle far more often than men’s.
secs.src: World Bank Global Findex 2025, via Data for India.

secs.t: ₹52 lakh crore paid straight into accounts
secs.s: Direct Benefit Transfer: cumulative amount paid, beneficiaries reached (counted once per scheme, so one person can count several times) and subsidy share
secs.r: More than 900 schemes now pay through DBT. Subsidies fell from 16% of central government spending in 2009 to 9% in 2024, partly because duplicate and fake ration cards and gas connections were weeded out.
secs.src: Government data via The Sentinel (April 2025); New India Samachar, PIB (August 2026); Business Today (beneficiaries, subsidy share).

secs.t: Seventeen years from an ID authority to a world payment system
secs.s: Key steps. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: The stack was started under one government and scaled under the next. Courts shaped it too: privacy was declared a fundamental right in 2017, and in 2018 private firms were barred from demanding Aadhaar.
secs.src: UIDAI; NPCI; Supreme Court of India; Wikipedia, Aadhaar.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Business Today (Viksit Bharat study, 2025); New India Samachar (2026); Global Findex 2025; RTI reply via Free Press Journal; UIDAI via Wikipedia.

06.take: India built public digital rails that reach almost everyone, including the poorest and women. Use has not caught up with access.

secs.t: Highway building tripled in pace, then settled near 30 km a day
secs.s: National highways built each financial year, km per day. Tap or hover a bar for the total.
secs.r: The pace rose every year to 2018–19, dipped, and peaked at 37 km a day in 2020–21. It has since averaged about 30 km a day, well short of the ministry’s stated ambitions of 60 and 100 km a day.
secs.src: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways via Deccan Herald (2019–20 to 2022–23), Business Today (2014–15, 2020–21, 2023–24) and The Tribune (2024–25); earlier years from ministry annual reports.

secs.t: The national highway network grew by 60%, open expressways 28 times
secs.s: National highways and high-speed corridors, km
secs.r: Over 55,000 km were added to the national highway network in eleven years. Access-controlled expressways went from 93 km to more than 5,000 km planned or built, of which 2,636 km are open.
secs.src: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways via Business Today (July 2025).

secs.t: Central capital spending rose sixfold
secs.s: Union government capital expenditure, ₹ lakh crore. Actuals except where marked.
secs.r: The Union government chose to borrow for building rather than for consumption. Capital spending reached ₹12.2 lakh crore in the 2026–27 budget, about 3.1% of GDP, roughly double its share a decade earlier.
secs.src: Union Budget documents; SuperKalam (2018–19 actual, 2025–26 revised, 2026–27 budget).

secs.t: The railway network went almost entirely electric
secs.s: Route km electrified per day, and the share of the broad-gauge network electrified, November 2025
secs.r: From 2004 to 2014 Indian Railways electrified about 1.4 km of track a day. Since 2019 it has done more than 15 km a day. By November 2025, 69,427 of 70,001 route km of broad gauge were electric. Seventy-nine Vande Bharat trains now run, the first from 2019.
secs.src: Indian Railways via The Week (January 2026); Wikipedia, Vande Bharat Express (August 2026).

secs.t: Metro rail in 26 cities instead of 5
secs.s: Operational metro and regional rapid rail, km and cities
secs.r: The metro network more than quadrupled to 1,095 km, including the first 55 km of the Delhi–Meerut rapid rail line. The annual central metro budget rose from ₹5,798 crore to ₹29,550 crore.
secs.src: Press Information Bureau (March 2026).

secs.t: Airports more than doubled; air travel grew seven and a half times
secs.s: Passengers carried by each country’s airlines, growth 2004 to 2023, and India’s airports
secs.r: Indian airlines carried 180 million passengers in 2023, against 24 million in 2004. Among peers only Vietnam and Turkey grew faster. Operational airports rose from 74 in 2014 to 166 in 2026, many of them small regional strips under the UDAN scheme.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (ICAO), air passengers carried; Prime Minister’s statement via NewKerala (August 2026).

secs.t: Ships now turn around in two days instead of four
secs.s: India’s major ports, 2014–15 and the latest year
secs.r: The average time a ship spends in a major port halved, from 96 hours to under 49. Cargo handled rose by more than half, and each berth now handles about 47% more cargo a day.
secs.src: Ministry of Ports via India Sea Trade News (2024–25) and Logistics Insider (2025–26, August 2026).

secs.t: Logistics now rated above Vietnam and Indonesia, behind China
secs.s: World Bank Logistics Performance Index, overall score, 1 (worst) to 5 (best), 2023 edition
secs.r: India’s score rose from 3.07 in 2007 to 3.4 in 2023, ranking 38th of 139 countries. It is level with Turkey, ahead of every South Asian neighbour, and behind China and South Africa.
secs.src: World Bank, Logistics Performance Index, via WDI. Pakistan, Kenya and Morocco not scored in 2023.

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Deccan Herald (2023); Wikipedia, Vande Bharat Express; NCAER for DPIIT, Logistics Cost in India (2023).

07.take: India built at a pace it had never managed before: roads, electric rail, metros, airports and faster ports. Speed of building has not yet become speed of travel.

secs.t: Solar went from almost nothing to the largest source of new power
secs.s: Installed solar and wind capacity, gigawatts, end of each financial year (March) and June 2026. Tap or tap or hover for values.
secs.r: Wind led until 2020. Solar then overtook it and has since added six times as much capacity. Together they reached 220 GW in June 2026, about nine times the 2014 level.
secs.src: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy via Lok Sabha answer (solar, 2014–2023); Mercom (March 2026); Energetica India (June 2026); Wikipedia, Wind power in India (wind, 2015–2024).

secs.t: A record 45 GW of solar in a single year
secs.s: Solar capacity added each financial year, gigawatts
secs.r: Annual additions stalled around 6 GW a year from 2018 to 2021, then doubled, and in 2025–26 nearly doubled again to 44.6 GW. India added more solar in that one year than its entire solar fleet in March 2020.
secs.src: MNRE via Lok Sabha; JMK Research (2025–26).

secs.t: Solar power became the cheapest new electricity in India
secs.s: Record-low winning bids for utility-scale solar, ₹ per unit (kWh)
secs.r: The winning price in national auctions fell more than 80% in a decade, to below ₹2 a unit in 2020, cheaper than power from most new coal plants. Competitive auctions, falling global panel prices and solar parks with land and grid connections ready did it.
secs.src: Powerline and Indian Infrastructure (December 2020); National Solar Mission and SECI auction results for earlier records.

secs.t: Third in renewables, ahead of time on its climate pledge
secs.r: India promised at Paris that half its power capacity would be non-fossil by 2030. It got there in June 2025.
secs.src: IANS and Mercom (April 2026); Wikipedia, Wind power in India; Drishti IAS (July 2025).

secs.t: Half the capacity, but just over a quarter of the power
secs.s: India’s electricity generation by source, 2025
secs.r: Solar panels and wind turbines produce power only part of the day, so a gigawatt of them yields far less electricity than a gigawatt of coal. Solar supplied 9.4% of India’s electricity in 2025 and wind about 4.6%. Coal still supplied about three-quarters as recently as 2023, a larger share than in 2004, because demand grew faster than clean supply.
secs.src: Ember Global Electricity Review 2026 via pv magazine India; World Bank WDI (IEA), electricity from coal.

secs.t: India still leans on coal more than most peers
secs.s: Share of electricity from coal, 2023
secs.r: Only South Africa among the panel relies more heavily on coal. China, which built far more solar and wind, has brought coal down from 78% of its electricity in 2004 to 61%; India’s share went the other way.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (IEA).

secs.t: Low use, low emissions per person
secs.s: Electricity use per person (kWh, 2023) and greenhouse gas emissions per person (tonnes CO₂e, 2024)
secs.r: Electricity use per Indian nearly tripled from 442 kWh in 2004 to 1,182 kWh, still less than half of Vietnam’s and a fifth of China’s. Emissions per person rose from 1.8 to 3.0 tonnes, about a quarter of China’s level.
secs.src: World Bank WDI (IEA; EDGAR greenhouse gas emissions).

secs.t: Factories for panels boomed; for cells, much less
secs.s: Annual solar manufacturing capacity, June 2026, gigawatts
secs.r: India can now assemble more solar modules a year than it installs. But modules are mostly assembled from imported cells: cell-making capacity is one-seventh of module capacity, and cells made up 81% of solar imports in the first half of 2026.
secs.src: Mercom via PV Tech (September 2026).

secs.t: Three numbers that need a second look
secs.src: MNRE; Ember; Mercom via PV Tech.

08.take: India built one of the world’s fastest-growing clean-power fleets and made solar its cheapest new electricity. Coal still generates most of the power, and most of the cells are imported.

secs.t: From most of the population to a small minority
secs.s: Share of people defecating in the open, India and the peer panel. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India started 2004 with the highest share in the panel, alongside Nepal. Both brought it down steeply. Bangladesh, Nepal, Vietnam, China, Sri Lanka and Morocco are now at or near zero. India, at 6.7%, is level with Myanmar, below Pakistan and Ghana, and behind Indonesia and Kenya.
secs.src: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, via World Bank WDI. The JMP draws trend lines between household surveys, so year-to-year changes are smoothed.

secs.t: Six hundred million fewer people in the open
secs.s: People defecating in the open in India, crore (10 million). One square = 1 crore.
secs.r: About 70 crore Indians defecated in the open in 2004, 44 crore in 2014 and 10 crore in 2024, even as the population grew by 32 crore. In 2004 India accounted for 59% of all the people in the world who defecated in the open; in 2024, 29%.
secs.src: calculated from JMP shares and World Bank population estimates.

secs.t: The change was in the villages
secs.s: Share defecating in the open, rural and urban India
secs.r: Nearly eight in ten rural Indians defecated in the open in 2004; about one in ten do now. Swachh Bharat Mission built more than 10.28 crore household toilets after October 2014, and rural India was declared open-defecation-free in 2019.
secs.src: JMP via WDI; Ministry of Jal Shakti via SuperKalam (September 2026).

secs.t: India’s own household surveys show the same fall
secs.s: Households using no toilet facility, National Family Health Survey rounds
secs.r: The share of households using no toilet fell from 55% in 2005–06 to 39% in 2015–16 and 19% in 2019–21. The fastest fall came in the Swachh Bharat years, even if the official “open-defecation-free” declaration ran ahead of the data.
secs.src: NFHS-3, NFHS-4 and NFHS-5 (Ministry of Health), via Deccan Herald.

secs.t: India moved past 28 countries
secs.s: Countries with less open defecation than India in 2004 but more in 2024: share in 2004 → 2024
secs.r: In 2004 India had more open defecation than 28 countries that now have more than it does, including Pakistan, Nigeria, Ghana, Laos and Afghanistan. India still ranks 36th worst of 182 countries.
secs.src: JMP via WDI.

secs.t: Basic sanitation more than tripled
secs.s: Share of people with at least a basic toilet not shared with other households, 2004 → 2024
secs.r: India went from near the bottom of the panel, with Nepal, Kenya and Ghana, to 83%, ahead of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Myanmar. 63% of Indians now have safely managed sanitation, where waste is contained or treated, more than Vietnam or Bangladesh.
secs.src: JMP via WDI.

secs.t: Piped water reached four in five rural homes
secs.s: Rural households with a tap connection, Jal Jeevan Mission, crore
secs.r: When the Jal Jeevan Mission began in 2019, 3.23 crore of about 19 crore rural households had a tap. By March 2026, 15.83 crore did, roughly four in five. A tap connection is not the same as regular, safe water: three-quarters of Indians have safely managed drinking water, by the UN’s measure.
secs.src: Ministry of Jal Shakti via All India Radio (March 2026); JMP via WDI (76% safely managed drinking water, 2024).

secs.t: Dirty water and poor sanitation still kill more Indians than most peers
secs.s: Deaths from unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene, per 100,000 people, 2019
secs.r: India’s death rate from unsafe water and sanitation, 36 per 100,000, was twice Bangladesh’s and five times Vietnam’s in 2019. Only Pakistan in the panel was higher. Toilets are the first step; clean water, handwashing and treated sewage are the rest.
secs.src: WHO, via World Bank WDI.

secs.t: Two numbers that need a second look
secs.src: Government of India (2019 declaration); NFHS-5; JMP via WDI.

09.take: India ended open defecation for six hundred million people in two decades, one of the largest sanitation changes anywhere. Ten crore people still have no toilet they use.

secs.t: Few countries improved as much as India in twenty years
secs.s: Development score, 2004 and 2024, 156 countries: income, health, basic services and schooling combined (0–100). Each line is a country. Tap or hover a line.
secs.r: India’s score rose by 26 points, the eighth-largest gain of 156 countries. Electricity, toilets, child survival and secondary schooling all spread fast. Of India’s neighbours, Nepal, which started lower, rose even faster; Bangladesh almost as fast.
secs.src: calculated from World Bank WDI. Score averages four dimensions with fixed goalposts: income per person (PPP, log), health (life expectancy, under-5 survival), basic services (electricity, sanitation, water) and secondary enrolment. Method in the Appendix.

secs.t: Basic services and schooling rose most; income per person least
secs.s: India’s four dimension scores, 2004 and 2024 (0–100)
secs.r: The biggest gains came from things the state can build and connect: power lines, toilets, school places. Income per person, measured on a log scale as in the UN’s Human Development Index, rose least, because tripling a low income still leaves it low.
secs.src: as above.

secs.t: Still in the bottom third: the other half of the same chart
secs.s: Development score 2024 against 2004, India and its 2004 peers. Above the dashed line means more progress than peers that started at the same level. Tap or hover a dot.
secs.r: The countries that most resembled India in 2004, Bangladesh, Nepal, Ghana, Kenya, Myanmar, Pakistan, all improved too. India pulled ahead of most of them, but Vietnam and Indonesia, which started ahead, stayed ahead, and Morocco did as well. Rising fast from a low base still left India ranked 104th of 156.
secs.src: as above. Peers: countries closest to India’s 2004 profile, plus Vietnam.

secs.t: Fifth by size, 143rd per person
secs.r: A country of 140 crore people can be a large economy while its citizens remain poor. Each success below is paired with a failure measured on the same data, and each pair points to what the next decade of growth should buy.
secs.src: World Bank WDI, 2024; UNDP Human Development Report 2025.

secs.t: Every success has a shadow; every pair of them, a remedy
secs.s: Read across a row: what India built, what it left behind, and how growth could fix both. Below: the deeper fault lines. Click to open.

leap.n: of 156: still in the bottom third

secs.t: Most targets need India to move faster than it did in the last twenty years
secs.s: For targets with a comparable 2004 figure: progress per year needed to 2036, against progress per year achieved 2004–2024, in units of each measure. Tap or hover a row.
secs.r: Out-of-pocket health costs, stunting and farm employment fell steadily; holding or modestly raising that pace reaches the targets. Public health spending must rise three times as fast as it did, and child wasting, which barely moved, needs a change of a different order. Manufacturing, women’s work and road deaths moved the wrong way for twenty years. Those three need reversals, not acceleration, and are the hardest promises on the card.
secs.src: Calculated from the baselines and targets in Part VII. Rate needed = (target − latest value) ÷ years to 2036; rate achieved = (latest − 2004) ÷ 20.

secs.t: Sixteen numbers to 2036
secs.s: Today, the halfway mark for 2031 on a straight path, and the 2036 target, grouped by what growth must buy
secs.src: Targets proposed in Part VII; anchors noted beside each. Halfway marks assume steady progress from the latest value.

secs.t: When each number can be checked
secs.s: A proposed release calendar for the data behind the card, 2026–2036; ★ marks a general election
secs.r: Some numbers come every year; others depend on surveys India has run late or not at all. If the Census, the family health survey and a learning assessment are not on this calendar, the card cannot be filled in, and the first promise to hold a government to is that they will be.
secs.src: Census per the Registrar General’s 2027 schedule; other surveys at proposed intervals. General elections due 2029 and 2034.

epilogue.take: India has shown it can build at a speed few countries have matched. The next decade will show whether it can make that growth felt: in a child’s height, a woman’s wage, a safe road home and air fit to breathe. The numbers will say. Citizens should be able to read them.

leap.n: each reached somewhere at India’s income, or promised by India itself
general elections and the halfway mark
with independent data, published on time

secs.t: Seven indicators, fixed goalposts, four equal dimensions
secs.s: Each indicator is scaled 0–100 between fixed goalposts, as in the UN’s Human Development Index, so scores can be compared across years.
secs.r: Indicators within a dimension are averaged; the four dimensions are averaged with equal weight. Missing years are filled from the nearest year within four years (eight for schooling in 2024), or by straight-line interpolation. Countries missing a whole dimension are left out. The score is a summary, not an official index; it is sensitive to the choice of indicators, which is why the chapters show each measure separately.

A rupee buys about four times as much in India as its dollar value suggests
secs.s: Income per person, 2024: at market exchange rates (current US$) and at purchasing-power parity (PPP, constant 2021 international $). Tap or hover a bar.
secs.r: Market dollars measure what an economy is worth to the rest of the world; they decide rankings by size. PPP dollars adjust for the fact that a haircut, a meal or rent costs far less in Delhi than in Dallas, so they measure living standards better. Comparisons of living standards use PPP; comparisons of economic size and trade use market dollars. The gap is why India can be the fifth-largest economy and still poor per person.

When two counts disagree, both are shown
secs.s: Examples of an Indian official figure beside an international or independent estimate of the same thing
secs.r: Official Indian data and international estimates often differ because they measure differently: police records against hospital-based models of road deaths, a national survey that counts unpaid farm help as work against an ILO model that standardises across countries. Neither is automatically right. Where they diverge, both appear, with the reason they differ, in a “contested numbers” box.
